text: Welcome, you are just a few pages away from hearing The Little Book tell its story.

This book is an autobiographical work based on personal memory. Some names, identifying details, locations, and circumstances have been changed to protect the privacy of individuals. Any resemblance to real persons, beyond the author’s own life and memory, should be understood through the subjective nature of personal recollection. THE LITTLE BOOK THAT WILL NEVER SEE THE WORLD

2 3

Who would I be if not for all the events that once folded themselves into my life and pushed me toward writing this book? The little book has held too much inside itself. Sometimes it even seems to me that it does not fully understand who it is or what it wants from life. Who is this little book? Why has it been searching for itself for so long, almost twenty-eight years moving through cities, rooms, people, fears, love, loneliness and memory? Will it ever find itself? Will it become calmer? They say a person is born already traumatized. I do not know if that is true. Maybe we are not born traumatized but too open to everything that will later enter us without knocking. I hope you found this book at the moment when you needed to understand that you are not the only book like this on the shelf. If you feel hurt or sad, the little book is always near. It will not give an answer to everything. It is not even very sure that answers exist in the form promised by adults, psychologists, religions and motivational quotes on pictures. But it can lie beside you. It can be silent with you for a while. It can open a page exactly where you thought no one would understand you. Usually people skip the prologue. But if you are still here then you and I are now inside my mother’s womb. The time is 23:40. Voices can be heard beyond the walls of the body. They sound muffled as if coming from another room through water. They tell me it is time to come out. Wait. I am almost finished. I need a little more time. I have not chosen a face yet. I have not understood what voice I will speak with. I have not decided what I will become: a boy, a book, a mistake, a miracle, someone’s son, someone’s problem, someone’s hope. Oh no. It seems there is no choice left. I am being pushed outward. The light is getting closer. The voices are getting louder. Wait. I am not ready. Although maybe no one is ever ready. Here I am. The little book that has just been born and has already started remembering everything.

Enerhodar. The maternity hospital where my mother first showed me to my family from a third-floor window.

5 4

I stood in the ashes and around me was a tribune. I was choosing my life and my family and then I entered my life.

6 7

***

I was born on March 19, 1998, at 23:40, almost exactly on the edge between Pisces and Aries. Formally, I could have been placed with one or the other, but now I think that border was the most accurate thing. Being between something is always a little uncomfortable, but later I understood there was a strange use in it. It was as if, from the very beginning, I was not completely in one place. Not fully there and not fully here. Later, this feeling returned to me many times in life, already in other cities, in other rooms, beside other people. I came into the world on Budivelnykiv Ave on a snowy night. The snow was falling in large, slow flakes. Maybe somewhere below the windows, snow creaked under shoes. Maybe car doors slammed. Someone adjusted a scarf. Someone held flowers in their hands, and the edges of them had already begun to freeze. I saw them almost at once through the maternity hospital glass from the third floor, while my mother held me in her arms. Down below, my family stood and shouted congratulations. Their voices rose unevenly, as if they were catching on the cold air, on the walls of the building, on the snow that kept falling between us. I could not really remember it myself, of course, but this scene still lives inside me. The maternity hospital was gray and severe. There was nothing soft or beautiful in it. It simply stood in the middle of winter with cold walls and dim windows. Inside, there were long corridors washed until they looked pale. They smelled of chlorine, wet rags, old iron, and that particular hospital air where there is always something of fear and relief at the same time. The linoleum on the floor was cold and worn in places. The lamps under the ceiling hummed evenly. Their light fell on the walls, on the ward doors, on the white coats, on the wet streaks left after cleaning. In the wards, there were beds with thin mattresses. The white sheets were folded neatly, as they often are in hospitals. Beside each bed stood a bedside

table with peeling paint, and inside those tables were small personal things: a cup, a comb, a bag of clothes, someone’s hand cream, a handkerchief, documents, maybe a piece of chocolate. My life began in that place, among chlorine, snow, gray walls, humming lamps, and the voices of my family rising toward me from the street.

***

My childhood took place in a two-room apartment in a nine-story panel apartment block. An ordinary building, the kind there were many of in small towns: gray walls, an entrance hall with the cold smell of concrete, a metal front door, stairs where every sound rose upward and echoed back. The apartment had three windows, and all three looked out onto the neon sign of a shop and the city’s main market. During the day, noise constantly rose from there. At night, the market emptied. The stalls closed, and only the blue neon sign kept blinking outside the window. It would appear and disappear, lying across the walls, the white tulle, the edge of the blanket, the floor, my hands. Each time, the room changed slightly because of that glow. For a second it was blue, then it became dark again. I fell asleep with that flickering, and it seemed to me that outside the window there was not a shop, but some kind of night machine watching the city and switching on its light only when it found someone. I grew up in love. In the smell of food, clean laundry, fruit on the windowsill, my mother’s hand cream, and my father’s cologne before he left for work. My mother often put that cream on my cracked lips. It was thick, soft, a little greasy, and always seemed to smell slightly of almonds. My room had four corners and one window. In winter, the white cast-iron radiator burned your palms. I still have a burn mark on my hand, a memory of my childhood curiosity and my brilliant desire to check how long I could keep my hand on hot metal. The radiator was heavy, ribbed, with paint peeling in the corners. In winter, dry heat came from it. There was a wooden desk in the room where I studied. The blue wardrobe

8 9

was packed with film cassettes. Two beds, mine and my younger brother’s. The white tulle covered the window, but it could not hide the blue light of the sign. The light wallpaper had a floral pattern, and in the evenings I found faces in it. If I stared long enough before falling asleep, they began to move. I lay there looking at them while the room grew darker, and the neon from the street continued to flash and go out. There was also a television in the room, the kind you inserted cassettes into. It was heavy, gray, square, with a plastic surface that always kept dust and fingerprints on it. One edge of the television was broken, and sometimes the cassette would not go into the slot on the first try. In one corner of the room, behind the door, there was a mountain of toys. Once, Grandma V. gave me an entire children’s kitchen. For me, it was almost a separate apartment inside the apartment. A little stove, little surfaces, little doors. Everything was smaller, but no less real because of that. I could stand in front of it and act out adult life and copy my mother. If you left my room, you immediately faced the toilet. To the right was the kitchen. Above the dining table hung a small television. It was always saying something, making noise, showing the news, advertisements. Along the wall stood the kitchen cabinets. On the floor was textured linoleum. It was slightly rough under bare feet, with a pattern that had worn away over time in the places where people walked most often. There were blinds on the windows, with broken little beads on strings always hanging from them. Those strings held the slats together, but they kept tearing. The windowsill was white, wooden, and served as a storage place for fruit. Apples, pears, oranges lay on it. The fruit lay right by the window, next to the glass. In winter, cold came from it, and the oranges became almost icy to the touch. From the kitchen you came back out into a small corridor. To the left was my room. Straight ahead, the refrigerator, with a pile of junk always lying on top of it: bags, boxes, some papers, small things no one wanted to throw away because they

might be useful one day. To the right was the toilet, tiled in black. A little farther on was the bathroom, also lined with glossy black tiles, where you could always see yourself reflected, only slightly blurred. White water stains remained on the tiles and never washed off. Later, a huge mirror appeared over the tiles, which my father hung there. Let’s guess whether this made it easier for my mother to clean the white stains. Spoiler: no. Hot water was supplied to our city by the thermal power station. We did not know what a boiler was, unlike people in other Ukrainian cities. A little farther along was a narrow corridor. Clothes hung on hooks. My drawings in felt-tip pens were on the wall. It was in this corridor that my mother curled her hair in colorful rollers before going out with her girlfriends to one of the four bars in our city. The rollers were pink, green, blue, with tiny teeth. I looked up at her from below and always asked her to take me with her to see her friends. She stood in front of the mirror, fixed the strands of her hair, painted her lips red, searched for something in her bag. The smell of hairspray filled the corridor before she left. It was as if she was turning into another version of herself: even brighter. I wanted to follow her, to be part of that evening life where adults laugh, talk, sit at tables, drink something from beautiful glasses, and know secrets children are not supposed to know. At the end of the corridor was the living room-bedroom of my parents. At night, my father slept on the floor, spreading blankets in layers, one over another, as if making himself a mattress so he would not have to lie on the hard floor. I doubt it ever became soft enough. My mother slept on a fold-out sofa that seemed never to have been comfortable. When my grandmother came to stay with us if my parents went somewhere, I prepared for the performance in advance. I made tickets, wrote the time on them, and gave them to her. She sat on that sofa in the living room like a spectator in the front row, and I prepared a show with outfits and dances. The curtains in the living room

10 11

served as a theater curtain. They opened the act and closed it. I came out, changed clothes, danced, announced something, disappeared behind the fabric, and returned again. The whole living room turned into a stage. There was a huge wardrobe in the room with ornate carving, gold inserts, and a full-length mirror. It was heavy, lacquered. If you moved the mirrors in a certain way, I could see myself in an endless number of reflections. It seemed to me that I was multiplying, disappearing, and coming back. I played with it, tried to trick the reflection, turned sharply, stepped back, came closer, watched to see whether the other me would manage to repeat after me in time. The television stood on a shaky stand that was held up by a wooden stick. And, as you can easily guess, one day it did not hold. The balcony was a glazed temple of storage for everything unnecessary and necessary at the same time. Everything that might be needed someday lay there: jars, bags, boxes, old things, tools, empty bottles, seasonal shoes. Poplars grew outside the window. In summer, the fluff flew, caught on screens, windowsills, clothes, flew into the rooms, and lay in the corners. From the window, there was a view of the DVD shop. My father and I went there together. A seven-minute walk turned into a real journey for me. We did not cross the road according to the rules because the pedestrian crossing was too far away. I remember the white tiled steps at the entrance, the white plastic door with glass. The shop smelled of cassettes. I immediately ran to the horror section. The covers looked at me with monsters, vampires, zombies, Milla Jovovich, and Saw films. I always chose films with vampires. I was drawn to them in a strange and powerful way. There was something beautiful and frightening in them at the same time: pale faces, blood, night cities, eternal life, which looked more like a curse but was still magnetic. They put the cassettes into a yellow transparent bag with the logo of some brand like BMW, and we walked home. At home, I climbed under the blanket, inserted the cassette into the heavy gray television,

and watched without looking away as vampires devoured people. I was scared. The most vivid evening happened when my parents went to visit friends. I put on Resident Evil with Milla Jovovich and watched it in complete darkness. The room was almost black. Only the screen flashed with white light. From time to time, I shifted my gaze to the end of the corridor, expecting to see movement, a silhouette, or a shadow. There was nothing there. Only darkness. But it was exactly that darkness that frightened me most. And suddenly the intercom rang. I froze. My heart immediately became louder than the television. I picked up the intercom. I think it was my cousin. I remember him as a person around whom problems often appeared: money problems, fights, and trouble of one kind or another. At the same time, he sometimes took us to the computer class so I could play computer games. Sometimes I had nightmares. I cried until my mother came. She sat beside me, stroked me, and took off my socks. My feet ended up in the cool blanket, and that made it easier. I became quiet, looked at the moon, at its pale light by the window, at the weak flicker of the neon, and gradually returned back into the room. Often, in order to fall asleep, I invented an imaginary show in my head. It was as if I was selling a pillow to customers over the phone. I explained how comfortable it was, soft, special, why they needed to buy it right now, what advantages it had, how it helped you sleep, rest, live better. I talked and talked, invented details, convinced invisible people on the other end of the line, and did not notice myself falling asleep.

***

Why was I drawn there? I was drawn to the place where there was something unknown, where I wanted so badly to find mystical signs and the feeling that behind ordinary life there was another layer, invisible but real. I looked at her and prayed with my palms pressed together, whispering my worries or my victories. I thanked her for them and asked to be helped further. To be supported in

12 13

something. To be guided somewhere. Maybe someone really did hear me, because I cannot say that I believe in the God shown on the icon, but I have always believed in something of my own. My face was lit in the darkness of the room, and while my younger brother slept, I whispered: “Help me make peace with him,” or “Give me strength for this.” The quiet night was sometimes broken by a passing car with music from discs recorded from pirate websites: new chanson and pop songs rushed into the room for a few seconds and disappeared somewhere behind the building. The magic broke, and the dark streets with the neon sign and a couple of streetlights at the crossing reminded me of reality again. I lay down and fluffed the pillow, imagining that I was trying to sell it through the show “Call Me at This Number,” and fell asleep, waking up in the morning to the words: “Son, it is time to get up for school.” The room was cold, with the small window open, because back then I thought that this would keep my skin beautiful. The air was fresh, almost sharp, and the blanket seemed like the only warm place in the whole world. I got up and went out into the corridor, heading to the bathroom, where it was always cold. Tea with lemon and sugar and a sandwich with sliced Doktorskaya sausage were already waiting on the table. It was the most delicious combination, and I still return to it now. Leaving for the stairwell and going down from the fifth floor to the first, I would meet the elderly concierge. After school, she sat with other elderly women from the neighboring entrances. They asked questions: how school was, how my mother was, how the family was, and they knew every resident of the building and the number of children in each family. Over the years, there were fewer and fewer of those grandmothers. The morning path to school began at six in the morning. This was the time the whole city lived by, because it was tied to the nuclear power plant and the people who worked there. I got into the car. It was cold too. My mother turned on the seat heating, and I sat in the back seat, looking at the huge number of crows sitting on the branches.

They made circles in the gray sky and settled back down again. The school met me with the warm yellow light of its windows.

***

Sometimes I woke up not only from nightmares. Sometimes I woke up from my father’s shouting and my mother’s crying. I heard them fighting. I was scared, but inside me there had always been this strange courage to walk into the fire. I remember entering the room and seeing the things my father had broken. My mother hugged me and cried as if she were looking for protection in me. I was too young to understand what was really happening, and I lay beside her, curled up into a small ball, feeling that with me beside her, she became a little safer. Despite their conflicts, I was lucky with both my mother and my father, because their attitude toward me and my brother was always special. I never felt deprived in any way, and I received enough attention. I think their conflicts still affected me. Sometimes a depressive mood came over me. I liked arranging my toys in a circle and talking to them, or spending time alone, inventing adventures inside myself.

***

Perhaps one of the reasons I fell behind at school was that my mother enrolled me in art school early. Almost my whole life happened there. The days stretched between easels, plaster mannequins, the smell of gouache, oil paint, and old wooden floors. I came home exhausted, with a slight nausea from the paints and the tension, and sat down with algebra notebooks or some other school nonsense that felt foreign and completely unrelated to me. Since childhood, my grandmother had taught me to make everything with my own hands. When my parents went on vacation or on a business trip, my grandmother L., my father’s mother, and I made cards for them. We sat at a table covered with oilcloth. She took out neatly folded pieces of fabric, ribbons of different colors, colored

14 15

paper, glue, and scissors with blunt ends. We cut out petals, made flowers, glued them to thick paper, and I carefully wrote a message, already imagining my parents holding that card in their hands. Then I waited for their return, and the waiting itself became part of the gift. I always felt good with my grandmother. Her apartment was calm and warm, like a soft cocoon I did not want to leave. There were no sharp sounds there. Everything moved slowly and evenly. We watched television with a small embroidered cloth lying on top of it, slightly yellowed by time. My grandmother took out old albums and showed me photographs of my great-grandfather and my grandfather, whom I barely remembered. He died of a heart attack when I was very small, and his face always seemed a little ghostly to me, as if he lived only in those photographs. In the evenings, we talked about everything and nothing at the same time. My grandmother slowly and carefully massaged my hands, as if reading the future from my palms, rubbing them with pine-scented lotion. The smell was thick, resinous, and real. I fell asleep to the ticking of the clock. I woke up to the smell of fresh, sweet pancakes already waiting on the table and to her voice: “Sit down, my dear.” Sometimes it was a fluffy omelet with two sausages shaped like a palm tree and placed in the middle like decoration. She poured black tea or hot chocolate into a small purple porcelain cup with a white saucer edged by a thin, shiny golden line. I held it with both hands, afraid to drop it. During the day, we could go out into the yard, wander there for a long time, find a puppy, and go buy pâté for dinner. In the evening, my grandmother lit a candle, and the soft light fell on her still-young face, full of energy. Sometimes she had conflicts with relatives, perhaps because of her bold character, which I think I also inherited. I inherited her habit of praying too. When my brother and I fell asleep, she whispered prayers almost without sound. Once I saw her praying in the kitchen and got scared that she would notice me, as if I had been spying on something very personal. Returning to

art school, I started in the younger classes, but I was moved quite quickly to the graduating class because I studied better than expected. It was there that I first sharply felt mockery and barbed remarks. People know how to envy, whisper, and defile things with words. That was when I first understood that intuition is not only a gift but also a form of protection, and I learned early to read people. I remember once my cap was thrown onto the roof, and my maternal grandfather, V., climbed up a ladder to get it. That is what the envy of small people looks like. My formal art education ended when my mother asked me to quit because my results in regular school were weak and a choice had to be made. But by that time, art had already settled inside me and stayed forever as something that is impossible to truly give up.

***

I am listening to Raga Jog Nadiyon, and it takes me back to that state when a light wind can be felt in the room from the half-open window, and the curtain slowly moves and touches the edge of the window, while the Christmas ornaments reflect the colored light from the lamps on the tree. In my grandmother’s living room, it smelled of fir tree, dried flowers, and something steady and long familiar. Her apartment, with Soviet furniture, was arranged as if every object had taken its place long ago and had no intention of changing it. Stone ornaments always hung from the mirror, and under it stood a chest of drawers where boxes and documents were kept closed away from my brother, my cousin, and me. That was exactly why we wanted to look inside again and again, carefully and slowly, as if something important was hidden there. In the bedroom, there were two large wardrobes, and when you opened the doors, a special smell came out, calm and old, with a trace of fabric, dust, and polished furniture. Her shawls hung on the doors. Her hair was gathered into a round bun. The hairstyle did not change for years. She wore wide-brimmed hats, long skirts, buttoned blouses or cardigans, and there was always a

16 17

silk scarf around her neck. In cold weather, it was a light coat or a fur coat. Before going out, she took out a small makeup bag, put on a little makeup, and that same scent of dried flowers appeared around her, which followed her for a long time in my memories. In the wardrobes, there was bed linen with the embroidered names of each of us: my cousins’, mine, and my brother’s. Each of us had our own blanket, pillowcase, duvet cover, and pajamas with initials. Sometimes we stayed overnight and slept in the hall on two sofas unfolded like double beds. In the hall, there was a dark wooden cabinet with golden metal inserts and a slightly darkened pattern on the doors. In the glass section, there was a special dinner set brought or gifted from abroad. The kind of dishes for a special occasion: porcelain, crystal salad bowls, thin cups with a golden rim, which were taken out rarely and very carefully. Books stood there too. Soviet editions, classical literature, almost the whole school reading list, and family photographs. In the evenings, my grandmother took out albums and showed black-andwhite photographs of relatives. Those who were no longer alive and those whom life had scattered across different countries. L. was from Kazakhstan, from the city of Aktau, formerly Shevchenko, a closed military city where an ordinary person could not simply enter. My father, V., was born there too, along with his two brothers, A. and S. In the early seventies, during the mass settlement of Enerhodar, her husband, T., moved there first with my father. It was considered prestigious. The state gave an apartment as a sign of gratitude for work and participation in the construction of a new city. Later, she left a high position in the Soviet party and moved to Enerhodar to her husband and son. For some time, she worked as the director of a kindergarten and raised three sons by herself because her husband left her and later died. The living room had light wallpaper and golden plaster cornices. There was a television with a lace cover, and white tulle hung down to the floor. There were many flowers in clay pots in the room. I

remember how we arranged fashion shows, dressed up in my grandmother’s dresses, put on her accessories, and walked like on a runway while taking photographs with a camera. I still have those pictures. From the living room, there was a way out to the balcony, where there was a cabinet with preserves: tomato juice, tomatoes with a light sweet taste, vegetables, dressings, fruit purées, and canned fruit. In every room, there were carpets with different patterns and colors: a dense red one in the living room and a calmer green one in the kitchen. In the corridor, there was a built-in pantry with groceries, and it always creaked when it was opened. In the kitchen, there were pale greenish cabinets. A wooden table stood against the wall, and above it hung an icon. There were also small porcelain cups in pastel shades from which I drank hot chocolate as a child, and a tape recorder with several cassettes. The bathroom had light tiles, a small mirror with a lamp, and the bathtub itself. When I stayed with her, I had an evening ritual. My grandmother filled the bathtub and added rose petals or dried flowers, and the air immediately became thick with scent. I lay in the warm water and relaxed while she made dinner. Neatly folded towels lay on the washing machine, and on the table appeared pâté, candles, tea with lemon, or a piece of hard cheese. In autumn, we went to the forest not far from her house to pick mushrooms. We took a small stick, searched for little mounds under the trees, and carefully moved the soil aside. There could be honey mushrooms or chanterelles, and sometimes whole clearings of fly agarics. After collecting a full basket, we returned, and my grandmother cleaned the mushrooms, cooked dishes from them, or made preserves. Enerhodar was surrounded by nature. There, you could get lost in your thoughts or go into the forest to regain your strength. But mushrooms were not her only talent. She knew how to make “Mushrooms” cookies from dough with glaze, and once she made a whole basket for my school. Everyone was surprised because you could not find anything like that in shops. In winter, closer to

18 19

the holidays, my grandmother invited the whole family to her place, and everyone gathered in her modest apartment around a large wooden folding table. Outside the window, light snow was falling, and the Christmas tree stood near the television with New Year’s programs. The same tree from which this memory begins. The main dish was manty. They were served on an elegant patterned plate, and the pink sauce stood in a sauceboat. I loved meat rolls with mashed potatoes and those same small canned tomatoes. Sometimes fireworks could be seen outside the window. There was champagne on the table in crystal glasses and children’s champagne so we could feel a little more grown up. After dinner, I remember the snow creaking under our feet when we went out into the courtyard of my grandmother’s building. Snowflakes fell slowly. My mother’s fur coat smelled of frost. A streetlamp lit the courtyard, and around us there was silence and the creak of snow. Then the car doors closed, the heater turned on, and we slowly drove to our apartment. Home.

***

The feeling of a rushing train begins even before you finally settle into your seat. The wheels are already beating against the rails, and the sound is steady and lulling, like the breathing of a large living body. The trains were always either compartment carriages or platzkart carriages. In a compartment, there were four sleeping bunks with soft mattresses. Two below and two above, facing each other. Between the lower bunks, there was a small metal table and a window with short curtains. Platzkart was a shared carriage with no partitions and many sleeping places. It cost less and smelled of food, other people’s bags, feet, and the road. But we are traveling in a compartment. There are several separate compartments in the carriage, with four people in each. A carpet runs along the corridor, and windows stretch beside it. When the whistle sounds, the carriage starts moving, and the light begins to slide slowly from one window to another, breaking on the edges of the glass

and creating moving shadows. The train gains speed, and I travel in an unknown direction with my grandmother. The conductor knocks on the compartment door and asks what we would like to drink: tea or coffee. Then he brings glasses in metal podstakanniki, with the initials of the railway company stamped into them. Everyone in the compartment begins preparing the bedding. They tuck in sheets and straighten pillows. If someone lies down earlier, the others unwillingly adjust to that person’s silence. If someone has food, they offer it, and a shared dinner appears on the small table among people who did not know one another that morning. The rhythm of the train works like a trance. The body rocks slightly, and you fall asleep on the upper bunk, carried away by that movement. My grandmother sleeps opposite me. At night, you wake up and look out the window. Beyond the glass, there is absolute darkness. The train is standing in the middle of a field, and railway workers walk along the train, tapping the wheels with a metal rod. In that moment, the comfort is felt especially clearly. You know that here, in your own compartment, you are safe, and beyond the window there is only darkness and endless unknown. Then the train starts moving again. The curtains move slightly, and you close your eyes again, as if under hypnosis. In the morning, the sun breaks into the compartment. The light hurts your eyes. People are already standing in the corridor and looking at landscapes that shift from forests to fields. Drops of morning dew slowly slide down the windows while the conductor heats water for instant coffee in packets, and the train keeps moving forward without stopping.

***

When my friends from the courtyard called my apartment number and asked if I was coming out to play, I would quickly get ready and go downstairs. The sun lit up our small courtyard. If you imagine the district, inside it there were these smaller mini-districts: five-story buildings with windows facing both the courtyard and the

20 21

other side. Each courtyard had one entrance and one exit. Each building had entrances and a small space near them, where elderly grandmothers or grandfathers usually sat. Every mini-courtyard had its own playground. Somewhere there was a broken slide, one swing, a concrete mushroom and some concrete dividers around it, the purpose of which I still do not understand. Maybe at some point there had been benches there, and all of it was supposed to look like a place to rest. But in my childhood it already looked more like the remains of some other era. Our courtyard, by the way, was not the worst. We had two whole swings and one slide. In the evening children came out of different buildings and we played with each other. One of the games was “robbers.” It was when some people ran away and hid, and the others had to catch them. Someone was a criminal or police, someone was in charge, and someone was just running after everyone without fully understanding the rules. You could hide behind entrances, behind trees, near garages, under stairs, in bushes. The most important thing was not to get caught and not to be the last one found. Someone would bring out Pokémon chips. They were also called caps or sotki. We played with them on the asphalt, compared whose chip was stronger, whose was rare, whose was shiny. Sometimes we hit them against each other or stacked them in a pile, and you had to strike them so they would flip over. Everyone had their favorite chips, and losing them felt almost like losing a part of yourself. Older kids could throw a knife into a tree, after drawing a circle and points on the trunk. We also played with firecrackers. We made a small hill out of sand, hid a firecracker inside, lightly covered it, and then there was a short bang. We called it a “puk.” Girls more often played “mothers and daughters.” It was a game where you had to build a family. Someone was the mother, someone was the father, someone was the child. They acted out different scenes and talked to each other the way they had probably heard adults talk. In winter the courtyard was divided into zones. We built barricades out of snow and played battle

for territory. Everyone had their own side, and you had to defend it until the end. But the most intriguing and truly daring thing was to go into the neighboring mini-district without telling your mother. Back then I felt grown up and brave. You walk along new streets, still very close to home, but your legs shake a little from the unknown. As if you had already left your own territory and entered another world where nobody knew you. I remember trying to defeat one boy. We fought, threw each other onto the sand, and I could never manage to beat him. He knocked me down again and again. I would go back to my entrance, gather strength and return to the battlefield. And he laughed. It happened maybe four times, until I finally snapped and went home. Back then defeat felt very personal. Sometimes there were strange moments in the courtyard too. Older boys could show adult things. Once a boy showed me how he pretended to have sex with a pillow. Another time someone made me show my private parts near the entrance door. Or behind the wall of one building, boys showed theirs. I do not think I took it seriously then. It simply remained somewhere in my memory as a blurry fragment of childhood. In some mini-courtyards there were small shops. They were called kiosks. There you could buy brick bread, which was called that because of its shape, and with the remaining money get something tasty for yourself. Gum, crackers, sweet soda, a chocolate bar, sunflower seeds. In summer I climbed a mulberry tree. The black berries were already ripe, sweet, staining my fingers and mouth. I picked the best ones because I was tall and could reach the upper branches. Back then I probably could not have thought that we were maybe the last generation to experience this courtyard phenomenon. Temporary tattoos from gum, which you wet with water and pressed onto your arm. Tamagotchi, which could die if you forgot to feed it. A sticky and stretchy slime that collected all the dust and stuck to the ceiling, leaving marks. Tetris with a grey screen and rubber buttons. A game console where you had to insert a cartridge and blow into it if the game

22 23

did not start. A choker on a girl’s neck, which back then seemed very fashionable and grown-up.

Swinging on the swings in my courtyard, I almost fell asleep. Poplar fluff floated in the air, the sun pressed down with its rays, and it was a kind of childhood meditation: back and forth, back and forth. There was no one to play with. Everyone was still sitting in their apartments. My father sometimes took me to the swimming pool. A big blue building, the entrance almost entirely made of glass. They took me there because of my back, to straighten it. A little later, my brother started doing professional swimming, and I often went to watch his competitions. There was an adult pool and a children’s pool. I think the only difference was the depth. It always smelled of chlorine there, and it was warm. Especially in winter, when it was freezing outside, and you walked in and there were immediately fogged-up windows, humid air, green plants in pots. At the entrance you showed a special card, which you had to get made at the hospital, handed your things into the cloakroom and went to the changing room. The changing rooms had dark tiles, metal lockers, wooden benches and old huge hair dryers. They were these hood dryers, almost like metal helmets from an old beauty salon. A large chrome dome on a stand, heavy, round, a little cosmic and Soviet at the same time. You sit under it, put that dome over your head, and the air inside starts to warm up. After leaving the changing room, you had to take a shower, and only then did you enter the huge space with white tiles, where sometimes there were patterns on the walls. I could take these special plastic things that helped me stay on the water, and I had to swim back and forth, that was how I trained my back. In some places the tiles were chipped, or they were already missing completely. My brother and I fooled around in that pool, and sometimes my father would spin us around and throw us into the water. Once, during one of those throws, I pretended that I had hit

the edge of the pool and did not come back up. My father jumped into the pool in the clothes he had arrived in and drowned his foldable Nokia 8800 Edition, which I loved very much. A button slider with a metal body and a slide-out keyboard. I always wanted a phone like that, but it was very expensive. After I finished swimming and my brother’s and my eyes had turned red, I would go back to the shower and stand under the hot water, washing my body. Steam rose upward and filled the room. It was a little scary to stay there alone, because the tiles bounced the echo back, and the sound seemed to spread through the whole space. You know that feeling of water falling onto tiles, when you are standing with your back to the wall, shampoo in your eyes and on your head, and while you are rinsing it off, it runs down your body, but it feels like someone has already passed behind your back. And you get goosebumps. After the pool, we usually stopped to buy a cake for my mother, because she loved sweets. She always liked it when we brought something tasty home.

Hi, Dad. So, little by little, I have reached you too. My father was the foundation of everything that held our family together, but I also think that it was my mother who gave him the strength and confidence to move forward and not be afraid of what he planned. As I have already written, he was born in Kazakhstan and lived there with two brothers. There were quite complicated relationships in their family. T. and grandmother L. both had difficult characters, and my grandmother lived through the break with her husband and then through his death. It seems to me that, from an early age, my father was forced to take responsibility for supporting his mother after the loss of his father. He graduated from a technical college in Kyiv, went to Moscow, worked as a builder, and sold pirated music cassettes at the market. At the same time, my mother was selling clothes on the other side of the market, and it was not safe because they

24 25

could be stolen by not very decent people who always appeared quickly wherever someone was trying to earn money. My parents met at a local disco in Enerhodar. He invited her to a slow dance to Roxette’s “It Must Have Been Love,” and that was the music playing during their first dance. My mother’s friend, N., also had her eye on him and wanted to invite him, but he chose my mother. After that, my mother and her friend stopped speaking. They danced, and after the disco, he walked her home. Then they sat on a bench for a long time and talked, and the next day they rode bicycles to pick walnuts. So, for almost twenty-five years, two months, and twenty days, they lived side by side, passing through the insane nineties, with banditry, crime, drug addiction, theft, raider attacks, total instability, the collapse of old systems, shortages, unemployment, hyperinflation, the rise of the dollar, the devaluation of money, and then through the crises of the 2000s in Ukraine, price crashes, financial shocks, and the constant feeling of uncertainty. I remember my mother’s story about how her parents exchanged their apartment for a smaller one to help my parents open their first shop, where they sold cigarettes, alcohol, and other goods. My father’s business went well because everything in the country was going badly. People were becoming poorer. The dollar was rising, and alcohol sales were increasing. Most of the time, he was at work. In the morning, light quickly entered the room, breaking deep sleep with his voice: “Good morning, my family.” The television was on with MTV. Music spread through the whole apartment. My mother was already making breakfast in the kitchen. “Where are my socks?” “Which shirt should I wear?” “I have absolutely no clothes.” “I look like a bum.” Almost every morning, my father got ready for work like this while my mother ironed his shirts under stress and argued with him about his outfit. He generously poured fragrance over himself, moving in circles from his head to his neck and over his body. Dolce & Gabbana Pour Homme or Dolce & Gabbana The One for Men Eau de Toilette. Those lasting masculine

smells stayed in the corridor of our apartment for a long time. Morning always felt tense and very dynamic. Always strong black tea. Always loose-leaf. Never in tea bags. In a piala, and never in a mug. Sometimes with a slice of lemon and sugar. He came home for lunch that my mother had cooked, and sometimes with flowers after another conflict between them. He looked classic: a polo shirt, a T-shirt, classic jeans or trousers, pointedtoe loafers, a watch on his wrist, and always a short haircut. In the evening, he usually liked rolling his socks into a ball, and later they could be found all over the apartment. He lay on the sofa and watched a film. On rare weekends, he tried to spend time with us. He took us into nature, where we made shashlik, or to the local health resort with a swimming pool and sauna. In winter, he took us sledding or tied the sled to the car with a cable, and we drifted through the snowy streets of the city. We rolled through the snow, and I lay there looking at the sky as snowflakes fell on my face. Sometimes he drove us to a slope near his office where children went down on sleds. With him, the feeling of safety and confidence was never in doubt. At the same time, his character was complicated and inherited from the family. He got irritated easily and could be sharp with us or with my mother, and I will return to this later. But he was a good father, who supported us in a masculine way without showing his emotions, even when it was hard for him. At least not in front of us. He worked constantly and steadily controlled the business and did not allow himself to relax even on weekends.

From first to fourth grade, I studied in junior school. It was a small two-story building made of light gray brick, with narrow green staircases and white wooden doors, and around it there were playgrounds, each of which reminded me of a small state with its own rules. The territory was surrounded by a fence, and it did not simply enclose the school, but seemed to hold childhood

26 27

inside so it would not leak out too early. We had two teachers. During the day, S. V. worked with us. She was short, with short light curly hair, very kind, and there was always something maternal about her. In the evening, T. N. came. She was tall, rather thin, with short dark hair, more modern and, at the same time, good-natured. The day-shift teacher taught all the main subjects, and the evening-shift teacher helped us do the homework that had been assigned during the day. Because of this, the school felt domestic and safe to me. One special thing about our school was that we had a duty schedule for who went to the kitchen to help with the food. Usually, two people were chosen, and aprons were put on us. We walked through the corridors. Along the walls stood pots with flowers. Under our feet stretched a long carpet. White tulle made the light muted. Large metal windows looked cold. There was stucco on the ceiling, and long round lamps hung above our heads. As we approached the principal’s office, the carpet changed color from green to burgundy. The smell of food spread through the school. It appeared before you reached the kitchen, and already in the corridor, hunger woke up inside you. We came to the little window, gave a slip of paper with the class number, and through the window they handed us food on trays, which we had to carry back to the classroom. Back then, it seemed incredibly responsible, and you felt as if you were doing something serious in your life. You carried the tray and watched every movement so nothing would spill. A normal school day lasted from seven in the morning until eight in the evening. We had breakfast, lunch, and dinner. We studied, walked in the yard, and did homework, which the second teacher managed to explain and check during the day. In the evening, my mother picked me up from school, and I ran to her to hug her. She always smelled special. The floral scent of Estée Lauder Pleasures and the frosty smell of her fur coat. That smell still lives in me as a warm feeling of elegance, like roses with thorns, like a lipstick mark on a cup and mint chewing gum in a bag. She had a folding

gold phone with a pattern and flowers, long light wavy hair, and red lips that made her noticeable among the gray city. She always stood apart from all the women in my city. She had a graceful figure and a sense of style, and even the way she walked, held her bag, smiled, and greeted people. Sometimes she said that we would not go home, but to my cousin’s place, and then it was a real celebration for me. At my cousin’s place, we played computer games on VKontakte or played with Barbie and staged dramas among the dolls. I could create a drama if I did not get the toy I wanted, and as my mother said, I was not an easy child. I could stay overnight at my cousin’s place, and we built a house out of pillows and blankets, hid from adults, dragged different things inside, and turned our cotton palace into a real shelter. Sometimes my cousin stayed at my place, which happened very rarely, but when it did, we watched Scooby-Doo. Right. School. That was where my first love appeared. A sweet, short girl who wrote poems about love. She gave me a whole notebook of poems dedicated to our love. I called her every twenty minutes, and now I think I probably irritated her terribly. I remember someone wrote a rumor on a piece of paper and gave it to the teacher, as if we had kissed somewhere in the school yard. This happened exactly when, in fourth grade, we were allowed to make a circle around the school. Before that, the world ended at the playground, beyond which we were not allowed to go. And the circle around the school was a small freedom. You walked along the wall, turned corners, saw the school from another side, and understood for the first time that a building had a back and that the world was not flat. The kiss may not have happened, but the rumor was stronger than the fact. After that story, we were forbidden to walk around the school. Those were the rules. Maybe that was the reason I became gay, because even then I truly felt slander around my pure person. Joke. In general, I was never deprived of attention from girls. Secret love notes were passed to me, and boxes of chocolates were placed in my locker for changing

28 29

clothes when I came to school in the morning. Only now do I understand that that girl could hardly have bought them herself and most likely asked her parents for them. But I remember something else. I remember how I suddenly became interested in black magic. I had animal bones, some amulets, secret notes, and a black box, which I buried on the school grounds. It was my secret. I also began to enjoy climbing trees. It became a real passion. I sat in a tree for the whole break and looked down at people. I showed my friends how quickly I could climb, and they tried to repeat it. During that period, perhaps at the beginning of puberty, I distanced myself from many people and went through a depressive state, which my classmates and homeroom teacher noticed. I drew crosses and graves during lessons. I cannot now remember the exact reason for that state. I do not know whether my parents were told about it, but I remember the moment when my mother found a notebook where I had written rough things about people who had hurt me or about a teacher who gave me bad grades. My mother was shocked that I was even capable of thinking like that, being angry like that, writing like that. The years in junior school went on. Games of cops and robbers and hide-andseek were replaced by W.I.T.C.H., where the girls imagined what kind of enchantresses they would be. And I watched Lemony Snicket’s A Series of Unfortunate Events on videotape, got inspired by Count O., and played him with friends, entering the role of a villain as if it were my profession. I always liked villains. As a child, I invented a profession for myself as a vampire with a castle where I had taken the school principal. I once said this at a celebration, and everyone laughed because children usually want to be firefighters or veterinarians, and I was not interested in being someone banal. A little later, the Joker became my hero. I began to understand that there is sincerity and honesty in villains. They do not hide who they are, and they do not become villains all at once. On the eve of the New Year holidays, our parents came to watch our New Year

performance, which we had been preparing all December. The assembly hall was decorated with tinsel, paper snowflakes, and toys. There was a small piano there, and dance lessons and concerts took place there. For three years in a row, I performed in a bear costume, and in the fourth year, I changed it to a king costume. I wore a golden crown with crystals, a long red cloak, red trousers, and a white silk shirt decorated with stones. We had to learn little poems and recite them to our parents or to Father Frost in order to receive a box of chocolates. As an adult, I learned that those boxes of chocolates for schools were organized by my father. But back then, I was not interested in that. I did not know that Father Frost did not exist and that he did not come down to us with a sleigh and reindeer. I did not know that Saint Nicholas did not exist either. The one who leaves gifts under the pillow if you open the window at night, and if you do not open it, then there will be nothing. For disobedient children, he gave out switches. By the way, the school held events every season where I could show myself creatively. In autumn, we had to make a composition from natural materials and create an art object. The school organized a fair where you could buy someone’s work. The principal herself became interested in my work, which I made together with my mother. When she asked how much I wanted to sell it for, I said for free, and apparently that was the kind of businessman I was. Definitely not like my father. But she still gave me fifty hryvnias, which at that time was decent money for leaves and pinecones painted with gold paint. If it was the March holiday, the hall was decorated with paper flowers, and once I stood out by giving each of the fifteen girls a tulip. In 2007, that was provocative and luxurious. When I graduated from junior school, I stood at the ceremony in a white tuxedo with highlighted hair, to the ringing of a bell held by a girl with a red bow sitting on the shoulders of an adult guy, and the teachers cried, wiping away tears and saying goodbye to us. And a little later, my younger brother went to the same

30 31

school.

I first visited Paris when I was eight years old. For me, it felt almost mystical. I remember exactly how we landed at Charles de Gaulle Airport, took a taxi, and I saw the beautiful church on Montmartre. Then we were brought to a hotel called Opera. It was a very small hotel on a corner. Some fragments have fallen out of my memory, but I clearly remember a red velvet chair, a spiral staircase with a dark carpet runner, and walls that seemed to be covered in fabric. The wallpaper had a floral print, with white branches. Our room was small, almost like an attic room. A coffee table, an armchair, dark wallpaper that looked almost velvety, a window facing the roofs of neighboring buildings. We lived on the top floor, because inside the room there was a wooden staircase leading up to a large double bed. My brother and I slept there. My mother slept downstairs, on a single bed by the window. The bathroom was on the lower level of the room. This room under the roof had a skylight. From it you could see the Eiffel Tower and those perfect Parisian rooftops, with their special color and shape. I watched people, and at the same time I felt shy about looking. In the morning, some man was reading a newspaper, a woman was watering flowers. In the evening, my mother went to the opera house for a performance, and my brother and I stayed alone in the room, watching Titanic in French on a small TV. I could barely keep my eyes open. I was falling asleep after a long walk. But for some reason, in the middle of the night, I woke up. The moon was shining brightly into our room. I opened the window, and you cannot even imagine it: there she was. The tower. It was glowing, sparkling, and I stood there with my mouth open, almost ready to climb onto the roof so I would not miss a single star on it. I shouted, “Mom, the tower is burning!” The moon was shining on my face, my imagination was too bright, and from that moment I felt like a vampire. I looked at the

moon and howled like a wolf: “Awooooo.” The next day we went to the main department store in Paris — Galeries Lafayette. Of course, I ran straight to the toy section, which, I think, was on the fifth floor. There were huge Lego boxes. I think my mother bought me a black Batman car there. We split up from the friends we had come to the department store with and stayed with my mother, walking around and looking at the shop windows. Closer to evening, my mother could not remember the name of the hotel. All she remembered was Opera. But in Paris, as it turned out, there were many things with that word, and that name alone was not enough for the taxi driver. Her phone was dead, and there was no one else to call. My brother and I stood near the department store while my mother walked in circles through the streets, trying to find the hotel. It was somewhere very close to the opera house, but every attempt was useless. It was already night, and the last visitors were leaving the department store. I did not panic, although I was scared. I tried to support my mother: I recited poems to her or sang songs so she would not worry. But I saw tears already appearing on her face. We had valuable things with us, and my mother was worried that we might get robbed. At that point, she had already decided that we would sleep near the department store until, maybe, her friends found us. She gave me her jewelry. You know, it was that time when phones still did not have normal navigation, and all you had was a SIM card inside a dead phone. And then suddenly, a miracle. We heard voices speaking Russian. It felt like something we no longer even hoped for. They gave us their phone, my mother put her SIM card into it and called my father. Then my father called their friends. That was how strangers from the street saved us. I remember the feeling when we returned to the hotel. I could barely feel my legs. I went into the bathroom to take a hot shower. How good it felt to end up in white bed linen, on a large sinking mattress, after almost believing that we would have to sleep outside in Paris. In the last days, we went to Disneyland for a couple of

32 33

days. Our hotel was in Mickey Mouse style, and the room, I think, was given in blue or pink tones depending on whether you were a boy or a girl. The most memorable thing was seeing that pink castle I had always seen in the Disney intro. And I was also amazed by the haunted house. It stood as if on a hill, with decorations in the style of The Addams Family: overgrown grass, dried trees, boarded-up dark windows. When we entered, we found ourselves in a small room with large paintings. Then the doors closed, and it turned out to be a big elevator going down. As it descended, the paintings started to become darker and darker. First, a girl was lying at a picnic with fruit, and then below her, skeletons, worms and cockroaches appeared, crawling toward her. Then you sit in a small cart, and it starts taking you through different rooms. You enter a ghost ball, and the ghosts fly above your head. A bride looks at herself in the mirror but no longer sees her reflection. She reaches her hand out to me. I was in complete awe. I threw a coin into the fountain so I would come back. Strangely, I do not remember the road back home at all.

Having a girlfriend in fourth grade feels strange to think about now. You are children, but somehow you already understand that you can be together not just as friends. Where does this idea even come from, that you need to kiss on the lips somewhere on a playground so that nobody sees? Or pass notes across the desks during class with texts about how much you love each other. You write: “Pass this to K,” and the note goes from hand to hand. Someone could unfold it and quickly read what was written. And in that moment you already feel somehow ashamed. How did we, as children, even learn to understand what love was? I remember buying a whole huge box of Love is… gum. You open a piece of gum, and inside there is a small illustration of a boy and a girl doing some ordinary everyday things, and the text says: “Love is…” For example: “Love is not worrying that you will

meet a new day alone.” And you open these gums with your girlfriend, you read them, you giggle sweetly, and yes, there it is, love. She wrote a whole notebook of poems about love. The teacher later read them out loud to the whole class and said, with a certain intonation, that those poems were too grown-up for such a young girl. And then, when love passes, the notebook gets torn apart, and the candies are no longer needed. There is your new lesson about what love is. It can feel huge while it is held together by notes, gum wrappers and a secret kiss on the playground, and then disappear so quickly, as if it had never existed.

As expected, after school ended, there were summer holidays for three months until September 1, and sometimes, even during the school year, my parents took my brother and me somewhere to Hurghada so we could lie under the sun, sit in the room in bathrobes, drink coffee, and watch the swallows when, in the evening, the warm pink sunset lay on the glass and goosebumps ran across my body from that light comfort, as if I were breaking through the matrix with my own feeling. But that is probably a story for later. When I was younger, I remember another piece of land and other holidays, which took place in Crimea. My parents arranged summer trips there from the time I was about five and almost until I was twenty, with different breaks, but Crimea still remained a large piece of my life that undoubtedly influenced me. Most often, the family went to Crimea, and I spent almost the whole summer there in Alushta. The road took about seven hours, and the road itself was like a separate chapter. First, there were flat stretches. The steppe was wide and calm, with a low horizon where the lines of the fields stretched like notebook lines, and sometimes it smelled of hot dust and sunflowers. Then the road began to change. It became more uneven, and hills appeared. Farther on, there were salt lakes, almost blinding in the sun. Sometimes water mirrors

34 35

stretched in the distance, calm and flat. Then the hills turned into small mountains and then into large ones, and you felt it not only with your eyes but with your spine, because the road became ribbed with turns, and somewhere inside, there was already a premonition of the sea, although the sea was not visible yet. And those turns up and down, when you suddenly flew out of shadow into sun and then back into shadow again, and somewhere ahead the mountains became larger and closer, and the ribbed road began to descend, and you understood that Alushta was about to appear. My father always opened the window when we first saw the sign “Alushta.” And the air there was warm in a different way, pine-scented and cool at the same time. The sky was mirror blue, and at night you could see the stars so clearly, as if someone had brought them closer especially for you. My mother always tried to explain the Big Dipper to me. She pointed with her finger and moved her hand across the sky, but honestly, I never understood how to find it. And it is even beautiful that I did not understand, because some things should remain elusive, otherwise they stop being magical. The headlights of oncoming cars lit the inside of the car from time to time, and for a second the faces became bright like a frame, and then disappeared back into shadow. Pines stood along the roads. We did not have an apartment there right away. My parents bought it a little later, and before that, finding the right hotel or rental apartment was often a great difficulty and took a lot of time. Usually, when entering the city, people stood with bright signs: “Accommodation by the sea, 300 meters.” But in practice, these were old tricks for tourists, and the Black Sea turned out to be nowhere near three hundred meters away. Later, when we bought an apartment in a seven-story building with a blue roof and a view of the mountains, everything became a little easier. Now that apartment reminds me of a real ninetiesstyle euro renovation, and in its own way it turned out to be cozy. White tiles with poppy patterns, red countertops, a living room with golden wallpaper and a

copper-colored sofa, a greenish room for my parents with colored stripes, and my room in blue shades. All the furniture was rounded. Nothing sharp. We had three balconies. Two looked out onto the mountains, and my balcony looked out onto the cemetery, and it never bothered me. It even added romance, because through the cemetery you could see the sea, even if only as a small piece. My brother and I turned our balcony into a play area and laid out many pillows there, like a Turkish palace, only ours and childish. In the morning, my father cooked us an omelet with vegetables: bell pepper, tomatoes, and onion. It was a heavy breakfast. Sometimes he made fried eggs with fried sausages, and then we got into the overheated car, lowered the windows, turned on the radio, and artists from CIS countries or something from chanson could play from there. We raced along the road to the beach, already with that feeling that the day would be long and good. Once, on the radio, as we were approaching the sea, they announced that M. Jackson had died. I cannot say that at that young age I really understood who he was, but the message somehow stayed in my memory. On the beach, I think the people who worked there already recognized us. There were beautiful guys there. They set up sun loungers and umbrellas for us, and all of this had to be paid for. My mother always took sun loungers with an umbrella. Our beach had a bar and a café where we got hot soup or a non-alcoholic cocktail, and then swam with an inflatable mattress or on a pedal boat, where you had to pedal and steer with a handle that looked like a stick but, in your hands, became a wheel. My father had a strange and funny habit. He could throw us overboard from the pedal boat and sail away with my mother while we had to swim after them with our arms and catch up. Sometimes we became bored of the same beach and tried to find a new one, but after unsuccessful attempts, we still returned to the old one. So the days passed, one after another, month after month. Closer to August, the big waves began, and we already knew it from the view from the window, from the way the sea looked

36 37

from far away, from some inner premonition. As soon as we left the entrance, we understood: today there would be a storm. The big waves were our favorite thing. My brother and I splashed around. We were knocked off our feet and tossed along the stone shore, over the small pebbles that did not hurt. I dived into a wave if I understood that it was too big and pulled my brother out if it carried him away. We were so happy that our lips turned blue and our fingers became like zebras, wrinkled and striped. It lasted until evening, until we surrendered, got into the car, and fell asleep from the salty air, the sun, and the seats heated through the day. In the evening, we got ready for dinner. The apartment filled with strong scents of perfume, and we went out to a restaurant called “Staryi Gorod.” There, a friendly waitress seemed to be waiting for us already at the entrance, and we sat in our favorite place on the balcony of the second floor and, almost knowing the menu by heart, ordered the same dishes. Of course, we did not always go to restaurants. Sometimes there were small street cafés under awnings where Tatars cooked national dishes: shurpa, pilaf, tokmach with chicken. It was so simple and made with such love that, despite all my fastidiousness, I closed my eyes to strange spoons or plates, especially after swimming in the sea, when hunger becomes stronger than you. The evening program was to walk along the embankment, jump on trampolines shaped like a castle or a dinosaur, play arcade machines, go into an inflatable obstacle maze, take a photograph in a knight or prince costume, or stick your head through the hole in a stand so your face became the face of some woman or man. Of course, sometimes my parents sent us home, where I watched Jetix with my brother while they themselves continued somewhere in a club until morning. My father took us on horse rides across the Chatyr-Dag plateau. It is the largest karst mountain massif, a yayla in Crimea, known as Tent Mountain because of its shape and pierced by hundreds of caves, including the famous Marble Cave and Emine-Bair-Khosar. Crimea kept mysterious pit caves and unique underground

labyrinths: Kizil-Koba, the longest one, Marble Cave, one of the most beautiful, and Soldatskaya, the deepest, with secrets of ancient civilizations, magnetic anomalies, and unique stalactites. Trips to neighboring cities of Crimea were special for me. Yalta. An incredibly beautiful city with white houses and sweet architecture. There was something mysterious in it. Many palms and pines, small residential houses, a long embankment so close to the sea that during a storm the water could reach you while you were simply walking and thinking about something of your own. Along the embankment there were attractions and luxury shops where my mother and father liked to shop. I adored it. I loved spending time with my mother, suggesting outfits and looking at price tags. Clothes hung beautifully on elegant hangers, and around them were large mirrors and proper light, and it seemed to me that this was adult aesthetics because in my city there was nothing like it. There were no beautiful shops, and nothing ever appeared there that could be called aesthetically attractive. After leaving with bags, we could go into McDonald’s, which opened in 1997 and was the first in Crimea. I was still small, and I saw the clown holding ice cream in his hand. I ordered a Happy Meal, opened the toy, and was happy about such simple things. On the Yalta embankment, music was almost always playing, and I remember how, in the evening air, a violin suddenly appeared, classical. The violinist stood as if separate from the crowd. People passed by, but the music caught you, and you walked more slowly. The notes flew into the open windows of cafés, fell onto the pavement, mixed with the smell of salt and perfume, and became part of a memory that is impossible to explain in words. Sometimes in Yalta, we could go to the Oreanda cinema if new premieres appeared. I took caramel popcorn, sticky and sweet, and those caramel crumbs stayed on my fingers. Artists often stood on the embankment. They displayed their paintings: landscapes of Crimea, cities, mountains, flowers, animals, cats, grapevines, roses, cypresses. My mother and I liked looking at these works. I liked how

38 39

my mother chose with her eyes what was beautiful. I was learning then how to tell real beauty from imitation. Learning how to look at the world not only as a child. The strongest and most exciting adventure for me was Mount Ai-Petri. We drove up there by car along narrow, winding roads, and it was tense because the roads were narrow and sometimes two cars had to fit on that road at a huge height. You sit there and feel your palms getting wet, although you are a child and as if you should not be afraid, but you are afraid. The mountain itself is 1,234 meters high. We went there in winter to go sledding, ride a snowmobile, and see the house of the bear that was hibernating. On the snowmobile, we passed the Crimean Astrophysical Observatory, and after all that, we could stop and eat shurpa at “U Seryozhi.” That was the name of the café. Sometimes we went up not only by car but by the Miskhor–Ai-Petri cable car in Koreiz. A unique cable car. The longest not only in Crimea. It was entered into the Guinness Book of Records as the longest span in Europe. In twelve to fifteen minutes, the cabin rises to a height of 1,153 meters, and the total length of the cable car is 2,980 meters. The route is divided into two parts by three stations: the lower “Miskhor,” the middle “Sosnovyi Bor,” and the upper “Ai-Petri.” And you ride in this cabin, and below you there is emptiness, air, and the trees become small. We traveled farther and deeper, and Crimea became not only a beach but also history. Bakhchysarai. A drier and more ancient city where history is not museum-like but alive, built into stones and courtyards. There is the Khan’s Palace, carved details, cool inner courtyards, shadow that holds memory. They spoke there about the Crimean khans and the capital of the khanate. There is the fountain everyone knows as the “Fountain of Tears.” And nearby, there are cave cities, old paths, lavender fields. There were palaces: Vorontsov, Livadia, Massandra. There were military cities, closed ones, as if they existed on the map but not in life. We also went to the Skazka Zoo, and I remember not so much the animals as a piece of forest inside that place. A

small area surrounded by trees, with one path that led to a hut. There was Baba Yaga’s hut, and it rotated 360 degrees, and Baba Yaga came out of it and called a child into the house. It was so realistic that I could not fit it into my head that it was only an attraction. It seemed to me that she really took children away. The hut stood as if inside a real forest. I was always afraid to go there, but still watched, because there is magnetism in fear. It pulls you like the edge of a cliff. Sometimes, returning from Yalta to Alushta, we stopped at the restaurant “Staryi Krym.” I remembered it not as just a place to eat but as the scenery of an eastern palace. This place on the South Coast was styled as an eastern palace with Crimean Tatar cuisine: pilaf, shurpa, chebureki. Inside there were carpets, dense, heavy, red and blue, low soft sofas, cushions of every color: red, gold, turquoise. The windows had colored inserts like stained glass, and the light passed through them not as a straight beam, but as something colored. The ceiling was decorated with patterns, and somewhere there were lamps and fabric curtains. Outside, the restaurant was decorated with ornaments, geometric patterns, and wooden carving. And to finish this chapter, I would probably stay in the moment when, once again, on the road back to Alushta from Yalta, which took about forty minutes, my father slightly opened the window to smoke a Parliament from the blue pack, and the rich smell of cigarettes appeared in the car as a strange feeling of prosperity, protection, calm, confidence, and a future that was still so long. Time moved slowly, and it seemed that everything was still ahead and you would have time to become anyone, even if for now you were only looking out the window and saying nothing.

In Ukraine, there are special days after Easter when people remember their dead and go to the cemetery almost as a whole town. Where I am from, people called it Hrobky, Provody, some said Radonitsa. Each dead person had their own small piece of land, their own little fence, a gate, a place where the family could sit at a table, and the grave itself, with its strange design on the stone. Some had expensive black granite with golden letters, someone had just painted the metal fence blue and it still smelled of paint, and someone else’s fence was rusting while artificial roses faded in the sun to the color of dust. Some graves looked rich, with marble on the ground and stone benches, while others were very simple, with a wooden cross, a jar instead of a vase, and a few sweets on the ground, showing the status of the family in their own way. We came to my grandfather’s grave and to my nephew’s, and then my mother would stop by the grave of her friend who had died in a car accident. Usually, when people came to visit the dead, they wiped the photograph, pulled out extra grass, fixed the flowers, sat down on the bench, and talked as if they had come

to visit someone, only the host would never come out to them again. People left sweets, cookies, Easter bread, eggs on the graves, sometimes poured a little vodka or placed a glass with a piece of bread on top. Somewhere nearby, people really set a small table beside the grave, took food out of bags, sat down, and remembered the dead right there. Children ran between the graves and collected the sweets that adults had left for the souls of the dead. I remember that strange feeling when you hold a sweet in your hand and do not fully understand whether you are allowed to be happy if it was lying on a grave. On the one hand, the adults seemed to allow children to take them, because the dead would not eat them anyway. On the other hand, there was something forbidden in it. Around us, people walked with buckets, wreaths wrapped in cellophane, plastic flowers. Someone called a priest to read a prayer. Someone discussed how much a monument cost now, how much they charged to install granite, where it was cheaper to order a fence, who made good tiles around graves, who had badly placed a cross, whose ground had sunk after the funeral and needed to be filled again. I looked at the graves and thought: on one grave, a person smiled from the portrait as if they had been photographed for documents; on another, a woman remained forever young, although beside her already lay her adult children or her husband; on a third, the portrait had faded, and the face seemed to be slowly disappearing together with the memory of it.
