I am twelve years old. The summer holidays are over, and together with saying goodbye to junior school, we had to make a decision that at the time seemed very adult: choosing the middle school where I would study from fifth to eleventh grade, almost half a lifetime. But in reality, it was not really us who chose where to continue studying. It was our parents. Many of my friends stayed in the school that was across the road from our junior school. Before admission, there was an entrance

42 43

test, after which we were assigned to class A or class B, and for some reason everyone knew that class B was considered a place for the “stupid” ones, although no one ever explained it out loud. In Ukraine, classes were named with letters, and I, either by luck, or because of my knowledge, or because of my father, who had arranged something with the school principal, got into class A and continued studying with the same kids and friends from junior school. The new school immediately seemed huge: a gray brick building with wide windows and a plastic sign with the name of the school, a cement inner yard with a couple of trees where older students ran around, and gates through which whole streams of people entered in the morning. Heavy brown metal doors and, behind them, a creaking wooden door let cold air inside. In the large hall sat the concierge, a woman with notebooks, a lamp, and a wooden chair that had sagged from long school days. A couple of plants in pots tried to soften the space, but it still remained gloomy. At the end of the hall, there was a chest of drawers with a mirror, very similar to the one my grandmother had, and near it, fourteen-year-old girls fixed their makeup, hairstyles, and short skirts before lessons. Then began the long school corridor, stretched out and straight. The ceiling was low, with evenly spaced fluorescent lamps, some of which seemed dimmed. The walls were painted halfway white and halfway a muted greenish blue. In places, the paint was uneven, with streaks. Along the left side stretched tall windows with white frames. Daylight fell through them inside, lying in long strips on the floor and walls, creating a feeling of emptiness. Under the windows stood radiators, and above them, narrow windowsills where pots with plants were lined up. The floor was dark, smooth, polished to a shine. It was always a little cold there. The sound of footsteps spread dully through the space, and even when no one was there, it seemed as if the corridor kept the presence of people inside it. The stairwells were tiled with a simple pattern or a chess-like layout of dark red and light beige. In some places, the tile had

been worn down to a gray, smooth state, and somewhere it had been replaced with tile of another shape or color, as if the school was being lazily kept in order. Passing the gym, the girls’ and boys’ changing rooms, and the cafeteria, from where a heavy smell of fried liver sometimes came, I turned right and entered the shared cloakroom, divided between the students of the lyceum and School No. 4, two different systems in one building. Metal partitions painted blue looked like bars. Hooks of different lengths held jackets, bags, and schoolbags. Here, I met my classmates. We left our things and went to our classrooms. Each classroom was arranged in its own way and depended on the subject. In geography, there were maps and globes. In biology, there were microscopes and posters with plants and organs in cross-section. We watched living structures move under glass and kept science notebooks. In geography, we had our own personal weather calendar, where we wrote down the temperature and cloudiness and drew special symbols. In literature, we acted out scenes from William Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet or went to the board to recite memorized poems by Yesenin and Pushkin. In music, we learned notes and listened to Bach, not fully understanding why it was necessary. There were many teachers, each with their own character, voice, and mood, and we had to adjust, read emotions, and sense the atmosphere. After every lesson, there was a short break and one long lunch break, when the whole school went to the cafeteria. It was a large room stretched lengthwise, almost like a waiting hall. The ceiling was low, divided into square panels with lamps built into them in even rows, giving the same slightly hospital-like light. The light was not warm or cozy. It was even. The floor was tiled. Rows of long tables stood strictly parallel to one another, as if with a ruler, with narrow passages between them. The tables were simple, dark brown, made of chipboard, with metal legs, and beside them were the same long benches without backs, where people sat shoulder to shoulder. By the windows hung thick tulle curtains with reddish-

44 45

brown valances. During the day, soft, diffused light came through the windows. On the tables, there were sometimes plates with unfinished food, mugs with drinks, and bread on napkins. You took a tray, and they gave you a side dish, a cutlet, and compote made from dried or fresh fruit. At the buffet, you could get instant coffee, three-in-one, in a glass mug with a large spoon for stirring, and buy pies or snacks with the money my mother had given me. Sometimes we went outside the school grounds to the nearest shop, and it felt daring and a little frightening, as if you were stepping into the real world. Back then, no one thought about calories, protein, or sugar. No one needed cappuccino with alternative milk, and no one felt that something was missing. Even the cockroach that once ended up in a classmate’s pie did not become a reason for screaming or outrage, just like the toilets without stalls, with a concrete floor and holes in the floor. All of it was accepted as if that was how things were supposed to be. After the school day ended, with no after-school care, no parents at the entrance, and no feeling that someone was about to come for you, we left the school, crossed the street and the yards, talking about something unimportant. And when I came home, there was an understanding that something had changed. This path would now repeat more and more often, and each time you would become a little more grown up without noticing it yourself.

Morning dew lay on the grass, and somewhere beyond the garden, a rooster crowed with the slow sunrise. The smell of fried eggs filled the house. The eggs were completely fresh. The hens had laid them that morning, and they hissed on the heavy cast-iron pan. The smell moved through the wooden rooms and quietly reached the one where I was still lying in bed. The pillows were dense and heavy, stuffed with rough hemp fiber. My head sank into them as if into warm earth. From the window, I could see cherry trees with large green leaves. Light

passed through them and scattered across the wall and the wooden floor in soft, trembling spots. These are my memories of food, of one summer, and of my second grandmother on my mother’s side. She was the softest of all my grandmothers. She laughed easily, sincerely, and widely. She knew how to catch your laughter and lift it higher, making it louder and more joyful. This place was another part of my summer. And perhaps a more important one than Crimea, than the mountains, or the childhood dream of the deep sea. It was the place where I pressed my feet into cool clay, ate fruit straight from the trees with sticky hands, climbed onto the roof of the shed, and shared my catch with friends from the neighboring houses. My grandmother and grandfather had a small blue house with carved shutters of the same color. Behind the house, there was a small garden where hens walked slowly. Under a tree stood a simple wooden table. Beside it leaned an old ladder leading to the attic. Relatives and friends gathered at that table. They talked, ate, laughed loudly, argued over small things, and then made peace again as if nothing had happened. Once, I put on my grandmother’s dress. I stepped into her shoes, carefully painted my lips with her lipstick, and came out to the relatives, proudly showing my outfit. In general, I had a habit of coming to her and trying her new lipsticks. At first, she laughed at it, but at some point, it became too frequent, and she gently said that it was enough. That I was a boy and boys do not wear makeup. My grandfather was stricter. He was tall and thin, with thick hair that had not turned gray all at once despite his age. His hands always smelled of metal, oil, and dust from old tools. He could assemble an engine and fix almost anything. Many times, I saw him repairing furniture, taking apart electrical devices, working with wires, screws, and tiny parts. They had a yellow Zhiguli that often broke down. It was in this car that they picked me up from my parents. The seats were covered with rough fabric, and on top of them lay wooden bead covers that quietly knocked against each other while the

46 47

car moved. That strange feeling on my back was part of the fashion of that time. The windows were always open, and warm wind filled the cabin while we rushed along the dusty road toward their village. Sometimes the car stalled right on the highway. Then it had to be pushed a little, and the engine came back to life. I remember evenings when my grandmother and I lay together under a blanket and watched Scream on the old television. Outside the window, tree branches moved, and their shadows on the wall looked like long fingers reaching into the room. My grandmother was also a very creative person. She embroidered cross-stitch and patiently taught me to do it too. I sat in a large armchair, threaded the needle, and pushed colored stitches into the fabric while she quietly corrected my movements. From threads, she created whole pictures. From beads, she made small sculptures of flowers, animals, and insects. The shelves in the house were filled with these little worlds made by her hands. She kept some for herself and gave some to us for holidays. She rarely complained. She loved plants, quiet morning hours, and small details that other people did not notice. She was delicate, sensitive, modest, and very warm. She and my grandfather had a good relationship. I never saw them fight. Between them, there was strong love, quiet, a little naive, and in its own way childlike. My grandmother’s name was V. My grandfather’s name was V. And perhaps it is logical to say that they had three daughters: L., Z., and my mother, O. Each of them inherited something from V. L. was the most emotional and loud. Z. was calmer. And my mother, O., inherited that same softness and taste for life. That delicate intonation of care and beauty, which later I began to recognize in her scents, gestures, and glances.

I have already touched on a small part of my mother’s story. I think that, in many ways, I owe the person I am now to her. I am similar to her in many ways, and we have many traits in common. She always loved looking

beautiful, and she could feel what was current and what was not. She decided to devote almost half of her life to raising me and my brother while remaining a faithful wife who listened to her husband. She could save money on herself but give us the best. She wanted to work, but I think that because of the Slavic mentality and the family structure of that time, women often became somewhat dependent on their partners. I do not think my father kept her at home, but probably, for him, it was important that his woman did not need to work. I think this came from the male principles and standards of that time. She learned to be a mother as she went, because she was very young when I was born, and she made mistakes. Sometimes she shouted, and sometimes she could raise her hand because of our behavior or poor performance at school. Now she sometimes tells me that she was foolish and that it was terrible on her part. But parents at that time were not as educated as they are now and did not have access to the resources we have today, so she took all her experience from the family in which she herself grew up. Her father was strict with her and with his daughters. There was always adrenaline burning in my mother. She loved extreme sports, loved adventures, and could pack a suitcase and rush with us to Crimea in the middle of the school year. She always attracted the attention of people around her with her striking appearance and openness to people. I do not think she was ever embarrassed to look funny or tried to seem like someone else. My mother always wanted me to look stylish, and I also paid a lot of attention to it, as well as to the mandatory haircut before the beginning of the school year. I could sit for hours in a beauty salon, flipping through magazines from the 2000s and trying to visualize those fashionable, unusual hairstyles on my own head. Of course, back then I did not understand that the models in the photographs most likely would never have styled their hair exactly like that, but I still pointed my finger at the magazine and told the hairdresser that I wanted it like this. And then you leave the salon smelling of cheap hairspray, and your egg-shaped head gives you no confidence in your own beauty. There, you could choose music for your profile, state whether you were married or not, fill in a questionnaire about your future or family status, subscribe to public pages with pictures, memes, or quotes for real guys, which boys showed off to girls. There, you could play games, collect music albums, keep a feed, and communicate endlessly. by a longer road, passing the music school, the boxing hall, and the hotel. Cottages stretched along the street, and my house was number eleven. I never told my parents about it. At school, I did not have many friends. Almost all of them were girls. It was always easier for me to find a common language with them, because topics for conversation appeared by themselves and did not require effort or pretending. Our interests matched naturally, and beside them I felt calmer and more understandable to myself. Two female friends moved with me from junior school, and later, around seventh grade, another one joined our group. I remember the moment we met very clearly. She was walking down the corridor in a beautiful, minimalist, dark-green mini dress. Her chestnut bob moved as she walked, and her heels struck the floor clearly, making her look even taller. There was red lipstick on her lips, neat black winged eyeliner on her eyes, and earrings in her ears. She always had a manicure. She smelled good, and for some reason I

remember that scent especially clearly. She came up to me and said, “Hi,” and I could not say a word. I just looked at her as if she were a girl who should not have been here, in this school, in these corridors. She really was different from many others, in her posture, in the way she carried herself, and in the way she occupied the space around her. I still think of her often, and I know I will definitely return to her again in the text, in memory, in the understanding of myself. At school, there were always small groups, closed, stable, and almost unmoving. These groups rarely mixed with one another. They sat together at the same desks, ate together in the cafeteria, and stayed together during PE. They were school versions of families, with their own rules, roles, and unspoken laws. Outside school, they also spent time together, and we were no exception. Each such group, of course, considered itself the coolest, and access inside was difficult. It required circumstances, loyalty, and points of trust. Sometimes even sacrifices. In moments of crisis, such groups could split apart. Dramas began, sides were chosen, and people were offended, but most often, over time, everything glued itself back together, even if someone temporarily left for another group. There were four of us: me and my three female friends. We went to each other’s homes to watch films and shot short horror films that seemed like incredibly serious projects to us. Sometimes we went to one of the few pizzerias in the city, where you had to call in advance to reserve a table. Later, a sushi bar opened and quickly became the essential place for celebrating birthdays. I cannot say that I belonged only to one group. I tried to maintain relationships with everyone. But sometimes I gave in to herd instinct and did bad things toward those whom my classmates considered strange. That is how the collective mind works. It can erase a person from the class, even if you sit at the same desk every day, or even if that person is a teacher. Perhaps the same principle worked with those boys who tried to beat me up. Maybe some of them did not want to do it at all, but

52 53

were afraid that if they did not play their role, they themselves would be thrown out of the herd, and then they had to participate just to remain inside. I think later I also played roles many times that were essentially not mine. I did it unconsciously, automatically, to be accepted and not end up outside, and that skill, or that trauma, stayed with me for a long time.

Black nail polish that was often chipped, dyed hair in different shades, and clothes that looked like school grunge. At the same time, there was some kind of punk energy coming from her, but she remained feminine and loved adventures. That was exactly what won me over. She easily agreed to get up early in the morning and meet the sunrise on the roof of a high-rise building with a view of the canal, or throw some kind of party at someone’s apartment. It always seemed to me that she could stand up for herself, and like me, she loved horror films. We could walk during summer holidays until morning, talking about all kinds of nonsense and not noticing time at all. I never would have thought that we would become so close, because once, when we were still in junior school, I kicked her to the ground because of some small thing we had not shared. I think it really hurt her then. But time passed, and it turned out that we had much more in common than I could have imagined.

***

There was a particular kind of adventure that belonged only to my father. On weekends, he would sometimes take me for a ride around the city in his white Mercedes. There was a small television built into the headrest of the front seat. I remember watching Jaws while sitting in the back seat of the car. The shark’s fin cut through the water while the city moved past the window in the opposite direction: gray panel buildings, kiosks, and somewhere ahead, the nuclear power plant, in the direction of my father’s warehouse. On his index finger, he wore a gold ring that could spin. If you looked closely, the center of it rotated separately, like a tiny wheel inside a bigger one. He wore a leather jacket almost yearround and leather or suede moccasins that always looked freshly polished. He carried a small leather pouch with documents and stacks of money, and in the car, in the glove compartment, there was a gun. His hair was cut very short, always at Ruslana’s. He spoke to people with a kind of respect that somehow still managed to press down on you. I do not know how else to describe it. He could say “please” and “thank you” and, in the same breath, make it clear that there was no other possible outcome. Sometimes, walking past his office, I would hear him raise his voice at one of his employees. Not exactly shouting. It was more like a controlled kind of pressure, when a report did not add up or something had not been done the way he expected. This was the border between the nineties and the 2000s. Back then, the words people use in 2026 for that kind of workplace behavior did not yet exist: toxicity, psychological pressure, abuse of power, violation of boundaries. There was no name for it. That was simply how bosses spoke to their subordinates, and everyone accepted it as a given, as the natural structure of the world. At the market, his people, that was exactly what they were called, “his people,” the sellers, although I never fully understood what made

56 57

someone belong to that category, knew him by name. The sellers had already set meat aside for him before we even arrived. It lay wrapped and waiting on the counter. After that, we went to a small cheburek place right on the market grounds. A place with the plainest interior imaginable: a plastic ceiling with office-style lamps, tablecloths in mismatched prints, some with animals, some with landscapes, plastic chairs that scraped when you pulled them out. Behind the register, there was always cognac or vodka, sold to go with chebureki filled with meat or cheese and fried in oil that had clearly already been used many times that day. In that unremarkable cheburek place, people with money and ordinary workers could eat side by side. It was not fashionable to stand out from your surroundings. You could not show that you had money. During the winter holidays, closer to Epiphany, my father would take a group of men, his friends, his partners, I was never sure where one category ended and the other began, to swim in a pond outside the city, at a country house. A priest was hired separately for the occasion, and everyone chipped in equally. There was shashlik over an open fire, pickles, prayers said before anyone touched the food. Usually, the toast was to our children. On the frozen pond, a cross-shaped hole had already been prepared, cut into the ice, and my father and his friends would dive into it. Then, coming out of the water, they would ask the priest for a blessing.

***

I always remember my father’s office as one of the warmest places of my childhood. These memories are connected not so much with work as with the feeling of a space where I felt calm. I would come there, and this place replaced a playground for me. Around adults, I felt freer and more confident than among children in the courtyard. The large territory felt as if it had been given to me. It was a concrete panel building with a long entrance for trucks and huge metal gates leading to a warehouse of about a thousand square meters. Inside,

there were many offices where people sat and filled out reports. I liked sitting next to my father in the mornings and watching how he calculated estimates, how he recorded family income and expenses in the old way, in an ordinary notebook. He allowed me to stay there, and I invented my own journeys across that whole territory. I could climb onto the roof, sit next to people who compared numbers, feed the fish in the aquarium, help unload goods from cars, or go with his employees to the shops and take part in unloading products. I liked walking inside the warehouse, between boxes, shelves, goods, and adult voices. I liked watching how the employees lived and worked, how they made instant coffee in huge mugs and discussed things I did not understand at all. I could take any drink from the warehouse and drink it while sitting in the big leather chair. My father’s office held many certificates, awards, and photographs with all kinds of people, from politicians to artists. In the cabinets, I found weapons, sabres or daggers, elements of Kazakh national clothing, strange souvenirs, and things whose origin I did not understand. He had a machine that cut paper into very thin strips, and I liked putting everything into it. I found crazy lighters in different shapes, from a golden one to a lighter shaped like a boy with a dick. He had a large water lamp with bubbles that rose upward in a spiral. I opened cabinet after cabinet, and there were more and more strange things inside. I felt almost like an investigator in that office. My father was definitely a music lover, because he had stacks of music CDs arranged along the wall. Large portraits of me and my mother hung on the wall. After the working day ended, I would set the alarm and rush to the exit, counting fifteen seconds in my head before it went off. I often cleaned my father’s office. Or more precisely, I had this strange habit of laying his things out on the floor in my own order: flowers with flowers, certificates with certificates, papers with papers. I remember once the cleaning lady asked me to stop tidying up, because I was only making

58 59

her work harder. In general, this thing with cleanliness had always been part of me. I followed it, and most of all I loved the moment after cleaning, when I could show the result. Set the right light in the room, straighten the curtain evenly, place things so that everything felt balanced, and receive praise. To this day, when something worries me or I feel anxious, cleaning helps me relax, as if I am putting order inside my own brain.

***

The city taught rules that were not dictated by glossy magazines. Here, it was a luxury to look your own way, just as it was a luxury to buy clothes outside Enerhodar. According to the 1989 census, about 47 thousand people lived in the city. In 2001, there were already 56 thousand. Then the numbers fluctuated, and by 2018 the population was a little over 53 thousand. Enerhodar is located on the left bank of the Dnipro, on the shore of the Kakhovka Reservoir, and the first thing you saw when entering it was a concrete arch with the word “Enerhodar” and the large city cemetery. Then came hilly sandy areas, pines, a winding road, and already from the highway, the first houses made of concrete blocks began to appear. They were almost identical and differed in nothing except the balconies, which residents enclosed, insulated, glazed, and turned into storage rooms, kitchens, or small rooms. Concrete was the symbol of the city: monolithic, strict, gray. The rhythm of life was the same. Entering the city, you saw five-story buildings of the same height and shape. In childhood, they seemed enormous, almost like skyscrapers, but with age they seemed to lower, and you began to feel taller than those buildings. Lower in height were small shops with aluminum frames and small windows covered with posters, price tags, and advertisements for beer, cider, and alcohol. Later, mini-supermarkets appeared where I went for brickshaped bread, told the saleswoman what I needed, and she punched everything into a calculator and counted the change out loud. There were shops that looked like

consignment stores, with tired goods, metal shelves, and dim light. All of them were located on the first floors of residential buildings, and if it was a separate kiosk, it always had a strict shape and did not stand out against the concrete development. In some sense, one could thank my grandfather for such a city too, because in the 1970s he moved here and took part in the construction of Enerhodar and the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant. The city appeared precisely because of the plant. Construction began in 1970, and the first power unit was put into operation in 1984. There are six of them in total, and in Soviet times it was the largest nuclear power plant in Europe. Together with it, the thermal power plant, factories, roads, and housing were built. And an important reason for moving was not only the prestige of the construction site, but also the chance to receive an apartment from the state. Sometimes my mother and I, out of curiosity, went into small clothing shops with names like “Anastasia.” At the entrance stood a mannequin with a piece of paper taped to it saying “New Season.” Inside, there was a dense selection of dark faux-fur jackets, suede boots and shoes, and the prices were not cheap at all for the city. But the owners did not think about service or development. Everything was limited to basic communication, and competition was almost not felt. The city lived slowly. The most respected people were considered to be employees of the factories and the nuclear power plant. They had benefits, vacation vouchers, transport passes, and in almost every family there was someone who worked there. The city was divided into seven microdistricts and had an adult hospital, a children’s hospital, a sanatorium, a market, and an embankment along the canal. The embankment was a special place: concrete canopies with arches called honeycombs, brutalist architecture, benches beneath the canopies, shade from trees, and the canal nearby. Walking with friends, you could go around the whole city in about three hours, from one edge to another, and by evening the orange city light lay on the concrete, making

60 61

it softer. There were many modernist buildings in the city. DK “Sovremennik” was a separate building with wide stairs and large dark windows. People went there for concerts, films, school performances, and graduations. Next to DK “Sovremennik” stood the cultural and youth center “Molodizhnyi.” It was there that a large mosaic about the life of the city and progress was located: workers, athletes. We were taken there on excursions and told about the history of the city, the profession of a nuclear worker, and the nuclear power plant itself. Sometimes the Pushkin Ball of our school was held there too: boys and girls dressed in gowns and tuxedos, and the school danced a waltz. There was an art school in the city, brick and restrained from the outside, but inside, a real greenhouse with large tropical plants, huge space, and glass windows separating different art classrooms. Enerhodar had its own hotel, “Enerhodar”: a high-rise tower with balconies and a low restaurant building beside it. At night, the glowing sign lit the nearby alley and the Victory Day monument. People came to the market from nearby villages and sold vegetables, fruit, meat, and dairy products. We went there with my father. Each seller had their own customers, and nearby stood unfinished buildings that never became either a market or a police institution. I remember when we still lived in the apartment and left the car in the parking lot, I walked home with my parents, sitting on my father’s shoulders, seeing the roofs and being taller than the trees. Sometimes I hid around a corner and scared them. I did it almost every evening, and it became my little tradition. In summer, warm light came out onto the streets, children finished their last minutes of play on wooden playgrounds, and their voices echoed in courtyards surrounded by buildings. In the Enerhodar forest, there was always a feeling of mystery. I listened to the sounds and imagined a girl, almost mystical, as if she were watching me from behind the trees, not frightening me, but simply being there. I leaned against a pine and believed that it took away bad energy. After

we had already moved into a private house, I loved simply running through the forest in an unknown direction without stopping, as if almost taking off. Sometimes the forest was dangerous. You could meet people with drugs there, and used syringes lay under your feet. Sometimes a circus or amusement rides came to the city, and posters were pasted along the main roads. All entrances of residential buildings were the same: concrete stairs, walls half white and half green, brown elevators with buttons and drawn floor numbers. If you were lucky, the elevator worked. Earlier, elderly concierge women sat in the entrances, women who knew everyone and kept order, but with time they disappeared when intercoms appeared. Since childhood, the number nineteen has followed me. Our apartment was under this number, and there were nines in my date of birth too. Over time, a typical apartment became covered with plastic windows, stretch ceilings with chandeliers, glossy kitchens, carpet over brown linoleum, massive wardrobes, plasma televisions, and fold-out sofas in living rooms where parents often slept while children were given a separate room. Flowers in plastic pots stood on windowsills, and glasses and dishes for birthdays and New Year were kept in cabinets with glass niches. In general, everyone in the city knew one another because there were not many people, and most of them worked at the power stations. Gossip was part of life. People discussed who was with whom, who had broken up, who was cheating. At the exit from the city, there was a sign saying “Have a good journey,” and every time you drove past it, it felt as if the city was letting you go, but leaving itself inside you as something heavy and warm at the same time, like a memory from which it is impossible to fully leave.

***

Enerhodar revealed itself best from the inside, through apartments, entrances, and courtyards, through familiar everyday things that seemed the same for everyone. The apartments really did look almost identical, as

62 63

if assembled according to one scheme. In the hallway, there was usually an old dressing table or a narrow wardrobe. The mirror reflected all that entrance life: a shelf with perfume bottles, creams, combs, leftover makeup, jars without lids, and random small things that no one threw away for years. These objects accumulated. The living room was the main space of the apartment. Along the wall stood a wall unit made of dark lacquered wood with glass sections. The sofas were usually foldout sofas, and parents slept on them. Chandeliers with crystal pendants caught the light from the television, and in the evenings the family gathered to watch the news or series. In those moments, the apartment had its own sound: the rustling of a bag, the click of a remote control, steps in slippers, the flush of the toilet, mouse clicks when the father played games on the computer after work while his wife cooked something in the kitchen and the child sat at the table learning the homework given after school. All of this came together into one even feeling of home. The kitchen, by the way, could have prints on the walls or cabinets: flowers, waterfalls, nature, fruit, or coffee cups. Sometimes it was very glossy, in a red shade, with a wave-shaped countertop. A table with oilcloth, an electric stove, a refrigerator covered with magnets and calendars. On the windowsill, sometimes dill or green onion grew, fruit lay in bags, and a thermometer hung on the window. Here, something was always boiling, frying, jars of preserves were opened and closed, kitchen utensils that were never thrown away spilled out, and dishes clinked. The kitchen was a place of conversations, arguments, reconciliations, and night teas or gatherings with beer and dried fish. In the bedroom, or in the room given to a child, heavy carpets with eastern patterns covered almost the entire floor. The pattern of the carpet seemed eternal. With your eyes, you wandered through it, studying it for hours as a child. The wardrobe held the whole flesh of the family: blankets, books, school textbooks, board games, and winter things. If there was an older child in

the family, then surely the mother kept the daughter’s graduation dress, and the son’s tuxedo was most likely bought a size larger so that another suit would not have to be bought later. In the living room, behind the glass of sideboards, there were dishes for holidays: dinner sets, glasses, crystal figurines. All of it was taken out rarely, only for special occasions. Sometimes strange small things stood nearby on the shelves: porcelain figures, souvenir vases, clocks, books, some small decor. Icons could stand in the corner of the room or hang above the doorway, and sometimes photographs of relatives were placed nearby. Every shelf and every photograph had meaning. Nothing was thrown away for years. Everything was kept and gathered dust. The floors in the entrance had their own smells. It smelled of someone’s cooking, and the light on each floor was different because the bulbs were changed by the people who lived there. The walls were always painted half green or blue and half white, and people left marker inscriptions on them with declarations of love or someone’s phone numbers. Mailboxes with torn-off locks, taped shut or simply open, were filled with flyers. Groups sat on the stairs, smoked, talked, laughed, or, on the contrary, whispered so the neighbor from the top floor would not hear if you wanted to climb onto the roof of the building. Small elevators with buttons to which gum often stuck, or where the floor numbers had been rubbed away. In the evenings, the concrete buildings burned with yellow light from the windows. In some windows, there was pink or purple light for plants. In the evenings, the city seemed to shrink, becoming intimate, almost domestic, and it was exactly this feeling that made it so memorable. Romance was simple and naive. Boys courted as best they could. Spraypainted messages appeared on the asphalt: “Forgive me, Katya,” “You are my only one,” “I love you.” Roses were wrapped in thick plastic film. People met by entrances, waited under windows, called so someone would come out and simply walk around the district. They made flaming hearts, took girls to the local pizzeria, or arranged

64 65

dinner on the concrete stairs of an entrance with candles and a luxurious plate of twelve pieces of sushi. Every weekend, wedding car processions honked through the city. Brides in white puffy dresses, grooms in light suits, sometimes with unexpected combinations, sporty elements, large gold rings, and glossy shoes. Limousines, short bridesmaid dresses, elaborate hairstyles with a large amount of hairspray, heavy makeup. Photographs against the background of concrete buildings, in entrances, by monuments, on a playground, in a park, near a fountain, or on the beach. A banquet with golden tablecloths, a huge number of salads that stood all day, assorted sausages, vegetables, chairs with large bows, and the main table of the bride and groom with an arch behind their backs, with balloons and many artificial flowers on the table. All of this in a café or restaurant with music, toasts, dancing, contests from the host, singing from a local singer, and, of course, the first dance.

***

I went to camp three times. The first time was in a small resort village called Kyrylivka, on the Sea of Azov, between Fedotova Spit and Peresyp. We sometimes went there because it was close to the Zaporizhzhia region. It was not the Black Sea, of course, but for many families, including families from Enerhodar, it was considered a more accessible option. As I wrote earlier, some people received holiday vouchers for exactly these kinds of places in Ukraine: Berdyansk, Koblevo, Odesa, Truskavets, Morshyn. The first time I went to camp, I was probably seven or eight years old. I cannot remember exactly whether my brother was with me, but I clearly remember the yellow bus standing and waiting for us while we put our small backpacks with things inside. Honestly, I always had some kind of lump in my throat when I left my parents. It was something close to a panic attack, especially if I woke up in the middle of the night and could not find my mother. I could leave the hotel room and start looking for her, walking almost

through the whole territory if we were away somewhere, or simply cry in the dark apartment from the most incomprehensible fear that she was not there. And there I was, sitting on the bus. It was hot, and tears were about to come. I felt uncomfortable with my peers. It seemed to me that they were too rough and badly raised. My first camp somehow reminded me of a sanatorium for pensioners. Buildings made of concrete panels, almost like the houses in Enerhodar, only two stories high, a separate slightly larger building where the cafeteria was, and a computer room. In camp, everything was always according to schedule, every hour was planned. Wake-up, breakfast, activities, swimming in the sea for ten minutes for each group, computer games, for boys the game “Mowgli,” for girls “Barbie,” then an afternoon snack, quiet hour, that was what they called the time after lunch and before dinner, when for a whole hour you were supposed to sleep, then dinner itself after sleep, an evening event, a trip to the toilet with the whole camp, and then lights out. And so it went for a week. A kind of prison. By the way, a funny fact: near our camp there was an abandoned prison with twisted knots made from bed pillowcases hanging from the windows. It looked as if there had been a mass escape. The wind blew sand around and rolled tumbleweeds across the ground. Our rooms were very standard and ordinary. About five beds, five bedside tables for each of us, one shared wardrobe, and a window. I remember being told that I had to clear the shelves because I had too many things in our shared wardrobe. Then I had to put half of my things back into the suitcase. My mother was very caring and had packed many outfits for me. After a couple of days, I was already calling her and asking her to take me home. I was disturbed by that system where we had to walk in line and live according to a schedule. The only thing that gave me inspiration was drinking kefir from a faceted glass with a pryanik. I always asked for more kefir and hid the pryanik so I could take it back to my room. I was always more interested in spending time with

66 67

adults and listening to them. I easily noticed details about my mother’s female friends: the shine of nail polish, a new haircut, a change of hair color. Somehow, it was easy for me to communicate with them, and they loved me too. In the evenings, camps were usually controlled by the older supervisors. These were people who kept order so that we would not make noise in the rooms. The boys from my room sometimes made noise. They called girls from the neighboring rooms through the hole in the socket or took off their underwear to spin their dicks like “airplanes” in front of the other boys. Later, when I was a little older, about fourteen or fifteen, my second camp was a camp in Crimea called “Mandarin.” It was a large territory with slightly better conditions, its own swimming pool, a cinema, and many different kinds of entertainment. For example, Neptune Day, or a day when the whole camp became “Monopoly,” and you could buy out one of the camp buildings. I was not much of an entrepreneur, so I preferred to take a bag of chips and lie somewhere in a hammock, and in the evening go to the cinema. Usually, after the evening program, the show for the whole camp, they turned on music for dancing. Of course, there were slow dances too, where boys showed their love for girls. Somehow it happened that I invited a girl from another group. Groups, or squads, were what they called groups of children or teenagers from five to eighteen years old, usually ten or fifteen people, who lived together like a big family for a while. There were eight to ten such groups in the whole camp, and they were divided by age. So I invited a girl from another group to dance, and the boys from my group, sitting on the benches near the dance floor, shouted something like: keep it up, man. Male solidarity. You received points of honor among your peers. After the dance, I went to talk with that girl near the fountain. We discussed some topics like what kind of dog you liked, or your favorite color, whether you liked the camp, and things like that. And the very next day, I told her that we could not date, which upset her very much. As I was later told, she cried

a lot, and her whole group comforted her. To be honest, I simply did not want to start those little romantic intrigues. For what? So that I would not go to the cinema alone, but together with someone, and eat lunches and dinners as a couple? Maybe I taught her a lesson that you should not fall in love so quickly with the first person you meet. It was also important to me that people were afraid of me, and it was as if I needed to build a reputation around myself, like protection against humiliation. And that was exactly what I did in “Mandarin.” I invented a story that I had twenty-four-hour security who watched me and the boys I lived with in the room. Because of that, people almost did not touch me. Neighboring rooms could often do some nasty things, for example spray you with something or pour something on you. Also in “Mandarin,” someone did the choking game on me for the first time. It was a game with breathing and pressure on the chest, after which you went into euphoria. Now, reading about the possible consequences, I understand that in essence you could have died from something like that. The third time, I went to another camp, and it probably became the most traumatic one for me. Because it was that age when you are no longer a child, but not yet an adult either. About seventeen. As if exactly that age is the most difficult, because the peers around you, carrying their own complexes, begin to play with the feelings of those who seem weaker to them. And even the fact that the camp was considered one of the best in Crimea did not protect me from jokes about my clothes, which were aggressively pink or green, because my mother always loved buying me something bright for summer. On the first day, usually, as a kind of tradition, you got to know everyone in your group, and each person told the others what they did and what they were interested in. And when I said that I made jewelry and notebooks by hand, I received mockery and sideways looks. I faced situations where the boys in my room went into my tablet and looked through my browser history, and there they caught me watching gay porn. Then they told the parallel

68 69

group and the group where I lived with the other boys in the room, and after that, half the camp mocked me for my preferences in porn. There, I remained a bit of an outsider, but probably for the better version of events, it was with the girls that I found a common language, and for them it was not a problem. Only now have I realized that, knowing about my supposed orientation, although at that time I myself still did not actually know who I was, there was a situation during a quest. It was a game where you had to search for answers to questions around the whole camp and find clues. Our group came to a task where someone had to kiss a girl from our group. The girl agreed, and they decided to choose me as the guy who had to kiss her. But I did not do it. Not because I did not want to, and not because I already thought I was gay. Rather, it was because of fear, because I had never done it before, and because of some young but already correct feeling that something about it was not right. Maybe that girl, caught up in the effect of the game, did not fully realize that she herself might not have wanted to make out with some unfamiliar boy either. How could we know that later this would not become the same kind of traumatic event for her as it became for me? I could not tell my parents anything, because then there would have been questions and, most likely, problems with my parents too. So all that was left for me was to endure until the end of the shift in that camp, so I could return again to my comfort zone among adults.

***

This city still gave me good people. And one of them was her. Our meeting was accidental: we began writing to each other on VKontakte. She was modest: long hair, a round face, wide eyebrows, an open gaze, and a light smile, as if it always stayed on her face. There was caution and delicacy in her, that special naivety that belongs to truly bright people. But that did not mean simplicity or emptiness at all. On the contrary, there was a quiet,

almost invisible energy around her, creating a feeling of calm and ease. With her, I felt strangely good. Every time I saw her, I felt light and a little amused, as if I were returning to a state where nothing had to be proven. I wanted to talk to her without tension, without roles, without the need to be someone else. It seemed to me that with her, one could talk about everything and nothing at the same time. Once, I gave her roses. Not because I was in love or expected something. I simply wanted something beautiful to exist beside someone, and I wanted to give someone warmth in this city. Once, we went to the Carpathians, to a ski resort. I was very young then and completely unable to flirt. And honestly, I did not think about romance at all. I still did not understand who I was inside. Until I was twenty, I lived playing different roles with myself, without trying to truly look inward and honestly answer the questions that already quietly existed inside me. I remember dinner at that resort: Ukrainian food, warm and light. She had long dark hair, and the light fell on it in such a way that her eyes seemed almost demonic, deep and magnetic. And in that moment, I felt one strange thing especially sharply: I loved her, but not in the way that was perhaps expected of me. I loved her gently, without the desire to possess. I loved her while understanding that I could not be the person she might have imagined me to be. In moments when I want to feel something alive, I try to talk to her. It happened once in Odesa. I called her and cried because what I felt then seemed like something very heavy, and her voice, almost like an echo, like a splash, returned hope for something better to me. You deserve to be part of my story.

***

Often, it felt as if I had to prove to teachers that I was not just the son of a rich father. I constantly felt some kind of prejudice against me. To hear from the computer science teacher that she did not believe I had made that presentation myself. Or to receive a

70 71

lower grade because my father had once not hired some relative of the English teacher. Or to hear teachers make little remarks about how I would be kicked out of school anyway, and even my father would not help me. And this went on through almost my entire school life, until ninth grade. On top of all this, there was bullying from students from the neighboring school. Gradually, a feeling formed inside me that it was better to be alone.

***

Sometimes it seemed to me that the world became bigger as soon as you left Enerhodar. The closest big city like that was Zaporizhzhia, about two hours by car. For adults, it could have been an ordinary trip for errands, but for me it always felt like a small exit beyond the borders of the familiar map. The road pulled the city out of me gradually. First, the familiar houses remained behind, then fields, gas stations, roadside cafés, and long stretches of highway began outside the windows, where the light lay on the windshield and the car seemed to float through dusty air. Often, the purpose of the trip to Zaporizhzhia was a haircut. My mother had a familiar hairdresser, M., and while she dealt with her own things, I quietly learned the basics of hairdressing by watching the master. The technology itself fascinated me: how the masters divided hair into thin strands, how foil flashed in their hands, how precisely the dye was applied, how the shiny mass from the tube turned into a new color on the hair. The salon always smelled of hairspray, ammonia, shampoo, and hot hairdryer. Cut hair lay on the floor, and several people were reflected in the mirrors at once: someone sat with wet hair, someone waited with a magazine, someone drank coffee from a small plastic cup. I loved watching them cut my hair or my mother’s. Some hairdressers had trophies on their shelves and paper awards in frames on the walls, won at competitions. The tubes of dye gave me special pleasure: squeezable, shiny, carefully arranged by shade. I also liked the tool bags fastened around the masters’ waists: dozens of different

combs, scissors, clips, brushes, each thing with its own purpose. We spent a lot of time in salons, and by the end of the day, hunger inevitably arrived. Then we went to the first McDonald’s in Zaporizhzhia, the one that opened on December 4, 1999, at the intersection of Lenin Avenue, now Sobornyi Avenue, and Metalurhiv Avenue. For me, this place was also part of the big city. I simply enjoyed the chance to be somewhere where everything looked different from Enerhodar. Sometimes my mother had more energy, and then the route became longer. We drove farther to Dnipropetrovsk, now Dnipro. This city felt even larger. It had more roads, more facades, more shop windows. The wide embankment of the Dnipro, Monastyrskyi Island, Lazar Hloba Park, long streets. A massive pedestrian bridge led to Monastyrskyi Island. In 2013, a decorative waterfall, 17 meters high, appeared there, and we went there with the class on an excursion. Shopping with my mother was a separate ritual. I could walk with her through shops for hours, look through the selection, give advice, touch fabrics, look at hangers, mirrors, light, and price tags. In good shops, the light made skin softer, fabric seemed more expensive, and the mirror seemed to promise you another version of yourself. Most often, we bought clothes in Dnipropetrovsk, and when I returned to Enerhodar, I felt like a white crow because of things that simply were not sold in our city. Returning to Zaporizhzhia, it was divided into two parts for me. On one side, there was an ordinary big city: shops, salons, roads, avenues, and people who lived faster than in Enerhodar. On the other side, there was DniproHES and the factories. DniproHES made the strongest impression on me every time. It was a little frightening to drive across it and see the enormous drop of water. At night, it was lit up, and because of that, it seemed even more majestic. Khortytsia Island lay below DniproHES, filled with history, Cossack heritage, legends, and the Sich. Zaporizhian Sich, Cossack kurins, Pokrovska Church, the defensive tower, the Museum of the History of Zaporizhian Cossacks. Nearby, there is a stone sanctuary more than

72 73

5,500 years old, and also Tarasova Trail. In the evening, tired after the road, shops, and salons, I fell asleep in the car while my mother drove my brother and me home. The inside of the car became dark, rare lights of the highway stretched outside the window, reflections of headlights slid across the asphalt, and shopping bags rustled in the trunk. I could wake up for a few seconds, see my mother’s hands on the steering wheel, her profile in the weak light of the dashboard, close my eyes again, and fall back into sleep. When we returned to Enerhodar, we arranged a real fashion show. I showed my father the purchases one by one, came out, turned around and waited for his reaction. And of course, in the finale, my mother came out in a beautiful outfit, as if putting the final point in this improvised runway show.

It was night. I entered a dark room, and inside there was some kind of black object. I began to feel anxious. The air seemed to grow denser, and there was a feeling of someone else’s presence in the room. Then I woke up, but the object was still in my room. Behind it, a black silhouette appeared. It started moving closer to me, and I suddenly jumped up, trying to protect myself. For a second, my body reacted faster than my thoughts, and then everything disappeared.

Days passed and turned into years. I grew up. My friends grew up. The subjects in classrooms changed, and so did the seasons and the rhythms of life. I sat on the bed by the window and looked at the sky and the dark forest ahead. The warm light of the lamp filled the room, and the tablet lit my face with cold screen light. I watched some shows on pirate websites and sometimes heard my mother downstairs making dinner. From far away, I already recognized the sound of my father’s car. It drove up to the house. The streetlights slightly lit the fir trees in front, and I saw him get out of the car and

walk toward the door. After coming into the house from work, my father loudly said: “I am home.” My brother and I did not run to meet him. Back then, it seemed like something ordinary. Maybe he replayed the same scene of coming home in his head many times: the door, the light, the voices upstairs, the children who no longer ran out to meet him because they had grown up and had become used to his arrival. Later, when I still went downstairs to take something from the kitchen, I said: “Hi.” We exchanged a few phrases: how are you, how is school. I never asked him how his business was or what was new. We did not speak especially closely. I could not share my problems with him, just as I could not fully share them with my mother either. In general, my father was a secretive person. With my mother, he was more open. They often sat on the balcony and talked there so my brother and I could not overhear their conversations. I think he hid many things from us so he would not worry us one more time. And my mother also did not always say everything about what was happening in their relationship. Sometimes I saw her with a bruise on her face. Sometimes she asked: “If I leave your father, will you stay with Dad or with me?” I always told her that she should look for what was better for herself and move on. I heard their shouting and saw broken plates, and sometimes cleaned up the shards the next morning so the cleaner would not see them. And closer to lunchtime, flowers could already be standing in a vase. My father could often lose his temper with us too. He was hot-tempered and could hurt sharply, ruin the mood with one word, and then just as quickly be in a good mood again, as if nothing had happened. He liked to drink, and I do not remember it always ending peacefully. I heard shouting and my mother crying when they returned toward the morning. He was influential, controlled the money, and could manipulate my mother through it. At some point, I noticed that my mother and father had stopped sleeping together, and my father moved into the guest bedroom. In the evenings, he lay on the sofa and watched films, and

74 75

when I came into the living room, I said: “Good night,” and went upstairs to my room. I went to bed and thanked the day for existing. My safe world became the basement. I went down there because I had my own small studio there. I dragged a table there, painted it white, and wrote handmade on it in large letters. There, I made notebooks or jewelry with my own hands. A couple of times, I managed to sell my work at school for a little money. The demand was small, but the very fact of selling made me happy. Maybe the entrepreneurial part in me really did come from my father. I remember how on City Day, which usually took place at the stadium with local singers and dancers, my father displayed his goods like other entrepreneurs, and I, at about fourteen, helped sell beer and snacks. I liked that feeling of business: boxes, goods, people, money, movement, conversations, the simple logic of selling, when you give something and receive something in return. But in the basement, everything was different. There, I did not need to be the son of an entrepreneur, a schoolboy, an older brother, or someone correct. There, I could simply make things with my hands and disappear from the house for a few hours while still staying inside it. Sometimes, while sitting in the basement and working on crafts, I thought about how my brother had already grown up. Suddenly, we were no longer interested in building cities from LEGO or staging a zombie apocalypse and destroying buildings. He was in his room, seemingly already grown up, but still among children’s wallpaper with an elephant and a giraffe. We somehow drifted apart without noticing. It did not happen suddenly and not in one day. I just went down to the basement once and realized that it had become empty there. Before, there had been two of us in our games, and then each of us ended up in his own room, in his own age, in his own fears. We were growing up. He had his friends. I had my own problems, and our interests separated. Because of school tension, stress, and my own helplessness, I often took it out on my brother and hurt him. Sometimes I also hurt him by not wanting him to

spend time with my friends who came to my house. I remember how at night we invented games, and I was your ride, lifting you with my legs while we tried not to make noise so mother would not hear. I remember how you told me about your problems at school, and I tried to help you, although I needed help myself. The end of ninth grade was approaching, a turning point for every school student. You either stay for two more years, or you leave and choose another path, finishing college or vocational school earlier than the others. I remember very clearly the evening when my father was lying beside my mother, and I said that I wanted to leave. My mother asked if I wanted to be a hairdresser. I was not one-hundredpercent sure. There was fear in me and a huge uncertainty. I found a school named after T. There were two of them: in Kyiv and in Odesa. We decided to go to Odesa so I could attend the school presentation. That was the first time I visited Odesa, but I did not really understand anything properly. The academy of hairdressing had an open day where you could get to know the school and its teachers. Now I understand how young I was then. I was moving somewhere almost without realizing what exactly I was choosing and what door I was opening. Teachers and friends gradually began to find out that I was not staying. And the closer the last day of school came, the heavier the feeling inside me became. I was leaving everything familiar, and at the same time I understood that there was no longer any sense in staying here. I did not see myself among these people, this school, and these streets. I remember packing a box of things, taking out books by Haruki Murakami, Russian classics, a photo frame with rhinestones glued around it, and a picture of me and my girlfriends N., D., and T. I began to cry a little. My hands shook from emotion. I was saying goodbye to the house, to the bed, to the rooms, to the flowers, to the garden, to the fruit trees in front of the house that I watered in summer, and to the forest. I walked through the city alone, and it seemed to smile at me. I had become braver and was no longer

76 77

afraid of it. It seemed to stop being frightening. Everything that had once seemed huge suddenly became pitiful, simple, and almost defenseless. I was waiting for something new, and at the same time, I was afraid that I would fail. I was afraid of disappointing my father because he was skeptical about it. I think my mother told him more than once that it would be better for me this way. Although how could she know that? How can anyone know what will be better for a child who still does not understand who he is? Why hairdressing? I do not know. Since my early years, I loved cooking and almost agreed to work in the kitchen of a local place because I was drawn to food and cooking. I often experimented and cooked for my parents and guests. I had a recipe book and found strange dishes in it that I tried to repeat. Then I wanted to be a dress designer. I told my mother that I wanted to have a house in a concrete style somewhere in the Alps and sew luxurious dresses. Then I wanted to be an interior designer because I bought magazines about renovations and looked through interiors, estimates, kitchens, and balconies, and told my grandmother what kind of kitchen I would make for her. What did Enerhodar teach me? Enerhodar is family. My father taught me discipline: to get up, to do, to keep your word, to count money, to not abandon what you started. My mother taught me caution. Not the kind of caution where you are afraid of everything, but the kind where you do not open yourself to everyone at once, where not every person comes with kindness and not every gaze can be trusted. She taught me to feel people before they managed to say anything. Sometimes it saved me, and sometimes it made me anxious, but in Enerhodar it was impossible without it. Enerhodar is nature and responsibility. Responsibility for the tree you water in summer with a hose, when the water darkens on the dry earth and the smell of dust, leaves, and heated bark rises around you. Responsibility for the lessons that need to be prepared for tomorrow, even if it is dark outside and your head is tired. Responsibility for your

younger brother, even if you yourself do not yet know how to be an adult. Even if you yourself are still a child who is confused, angry, afraid, and does not always understand how to love properly. I remember how you fell through the ice into a frozen pond, and I ran to you without thinking that I could fall through too. In that moment, there was no fear and no reasoning. Maybe this is how the adult part appears inside a child. Enerhodar is a school with the first knives in the back. There, I learned what pain is. When something seems to tighten inside, and then for a long time you pretend that nothing happened. There, I understood that friends can stop being friends, that people can laugh with you and then discuss you behind your back. There, I saw how money disfigures people, how it makes some feel higher and others smaller. There, I understood that beauty can irritate people, that the desire to look different can become a reason for anger, that being different sometimes turns into a reason for fear. But Enerhodar is not only pain. Enerhodar is the forest that smelled of pines, mushrooms, and my grandmother’s borscht. It is the garden where, in summer, branches bent under the weight of fruit, where hands smelled of greenery and earth. It is the basement with the white table and my loneliness, in which I tried to make something of my own, to assemble from paper, threads, beads, and glue proof that I existed. It is my mother’s breakfasts, the smell of tea and a sandwich. It is my father’s shashlik on skewers. It is the car at the gate, its familiar sound before it even appeared in the window. It is the office where it smelled of papers, coffee, the warehouse, money, and a leather chair. And it is the moon to which I told everything I could not say to people. The alarm rang early in the morning. I sat at the large table under the lamp. My mother made breakfast. It was still dark outside. My father stood in the doorway and hugged me. We packed boxes and suitcases and drove out of the garage. The doors slowly closed. I looked out the window as panel buildings changed into the same panel buildings, empty

78 79

streets, and lonely traffic lights. And then I was already beyond the city. I was driving into a new chapter of my life. There was silence in the car. In my head, there were hundreds of questions and an incredible heaviness from the number of memories, but at the same time, there was the feeling that tomorrow I would wake up in another bed, completely alone with the new life I had wanted so much. Enerhodar remained behind.

I am sitting on a plane. On the way to the airport, I could always tell my parents some scary dream about how we would crash. We are sitting in the car, I am in the back seat, and inside the cabin there is again this nervous atmosphere of my father, who is angry because we took too long to get ready or because we might miss the plane. He smokes blue Parliament one after another, opening the window, and the smell of dry grass, endless fields of sunflowers, cabbage or wheat mixes with tobacco smoke and flies into the car. Somewhere far away, the power plant with its two chimneys is still visible, and white smoke comes out of one of them. Now I remember how sometimes in Enerhodar they tested the alarm signals. The siren would start sounding, and for a second my friends and I thought that maybe something had happened at the nuclear power plant. Near our school there was a monument in memory of Chornobyl, and there we remembered the victims of that catastrophe. A city built around a power plant, with similar Soviet architecture, parks, fountains, wide streets, almost identical to Chornobyl. Why did I even tell those scary stories about the plane, when they were not true? My father always crossed himself when we passed a cross or a church. We often flew from Zaporizhzhia or Dnipropetrovsk. And now we are taking off. The plane gains speed, the pressure pushes me into the seat, and everything inside me twists. I usually say a prayer. Well, more like I just speak to someone above. I never imagined Jesus exactly the way he is painted on icons. For me, it was always some kind of energy

that cannot be described. I never had an image. And so I speak to him. Interesting, why exactly “him” and not “them”? I promise to be good, just please make sure we take off and land safely. I was afraid to die. That was how I ended my prayer. I am so high above the clouds. And essentially I am at the level where you usually turn when you ask for help, support or strength, looking up at the sky. And now I am literally here, inside my wishes, inside my anxiety, flying through the clouds. They are so fluffy, and the plane seems to dive into them. Then the desert becomes visible. Near Sharm El Sheikh, it is the Sinai Desert. And mountains, with snow lying on their peaks. The plane descends and prepares to land. But at some point it starts humming loudly. So loudly that I do not understand whether this is normal. Then it starts shaking a little and swaying from side to side. This is already happening during the landing. And suddenly — bang. The plane feels like it falls heavily onto the ground. The landing is so sharp that I almost jump out of my seat. My father probably went even greyer. We leave the airport and get into the transfer that is supposed to take us to the hotel. Most likely, as usual, we will have to sit at reception for another two hours while my father tries to figure out why, for the room with a sea view that he paid for, they are trying to put us in a room with a view of the neighbouring hotel. After two hours of arguing, of course, he will make an additional payment, and they will finally put us in a room with a sea view.

At some point, everything that had seemed like distant politics began entering ordinary life. On November 21, 2013, the decision by the president of Ukraine, V. Ya., to reject the agreement on closer ties with the European Union and turn the country back toward Russia caused the first protests. People went out into the streets. They were dispersed by force. The authorities passed laws that many called dictatorial, and the protest was no longer

80 81

only about the European path. Ukrainians were tired of being ruled without being heard. In February 2014, bloody clashes began on Maidan. I remember watching television with my father and mother, and we could not believe that this was happening. The country seemed to crack open. President V. Ya. fled Ukraine. Society was in shock. The state was suddenly without a president, and Kyiv, the heart of Ukraine, was burning through Maidan, with hundreds of people killed by dictatorial rule. It was at that moment that Russia used the weakness of the new Ukrainian government and began the seizure of Crimea. In Crimea, many people saw the removal of V. Ya. as a coup. Russian media pressed on fears, Russian special services pushed the situation, and part of society quickly turned against the new leadership of Ukraine. The Mejlis of the Crimean Tatar people, on the contrary, supported the new Ukrainian government and later refused to recognize the Crimean referendum as legal. Russian soldiers without insignia entered Crimea, and no one could stop them because, after the previous government, everything had either been sold off or looted. On February 27, Russian special forces seized the buildings of the authorities of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. In the seized parliament, a session was held, after which a new Crimean government appeared, headed by S. A., and it was not recognized by the central authorities of Ukraine. On March 1, the Federation Council of Russia allowed President V. P. to use troops on the territory of Ukraine, although in fact, they were already there. On March 16, a referendum on the status of the peninsula was held in Crimea. It was organized under military control, and Ukraine did not recognize it as legal. On March 18, Russia formally announced the inclusion of Crimea into its territory and, from March 19 to March 25, completed the seizure of the remaining Ukrainian military bases. By March 26, Russia already had full military control over the peninsula. Ukraine did not recognize the annexation and began speaking of Crimea as a temporarily occupied territory. Western countries excluded Russia

from the G8 and began imposing sanctions. This was the beginning of the undeclared Russian-Ukrainian war. Since 2014, Ukraine has begun a diplomatic struggle for the return of Crimea. Ukraine was still standing with an open wound, not knowing how to live after Maidan, the flight of V. Ya., and the seizure of the peninsula, while in the east, another movement was already beginning. Donbas, Donetsk, Luhansk, cities of mines, factories, slag heaps, and people used to hard work in mines and at huge plants. I remember how everyone talked about it in Enerhodar, but it still felt like something happening somewhere far away. In April 2014, pro-Russian forces and groups supported by Russia began seizing administrative buildings in Donetsk and Luhansk regions. In May 2014, so-called referendums were held in Donetsk and Luhansk, which Ukraine and most of the international community did not recognize as legal. After them, “DNR” and “LNR” were declared. By the summer of 2014, the war in the east had become a real armed conflict. Ukrainian forces began an operation against the armed groups, and Russia denied direct involvement, although international organizations and researchers pointed to the flow of weapons, people, and support across the Russian border. By 2015, the Minsk agreements appeared, along with a frozen and, at the same time, not frozen state of war. Formally, people spoke about ceasefires, but people continued to die.

Once I decided to take a dagger with me. The same one from my father’s office. And there I was, in a blue cashmere coat, with a dagger inside my backpack, which, honestly, I had almost forgotten about, walking straight into the arch where the police were standing. They were guarding Maidan on the Day of the Heavenly Hundred, the people who died during the revolution and the overthrow of V. Ya.’s government. They stopped me and started searching for me. They were doing it for safety, to prevent terrorist attacks or something like that. They opened my backpack, and there was the knife.

82 83

Wow. I did not even know what to say to them. When they asked, “Why do you have a knife?”. The only thing I could answer was something like, “For self-defense.” They asked where I was going. I said I was going to get croissants at TSUM. TSUM is this luxurious department store with brands. I also told them that I had a return ticket to Odesa. Sounds like a guy who was definitely planning to commit an attack and leave the city the same day, right? Journalists started surrounding me from all sides, giving me business cards and asking me to write to them later and tell them what happened. They took me to the police station, and I wrote a huge statement explaining what I was doing, where I was going, why I had a dagger, and what exactly I was trying to do. I begged them to let me go because I had a train to Odesa. Somehow, by some miracle, they did. They kept the knife. Of course, the story did not end there. I called my mother and told her what a good job I had done getting out of the police station, assuring her that everything was okay. Although, honestly, there was nothing okay about that situation. After some time, the same police started calling me again, now with threats. They said that if I did not appear in court, they could assign me to some kind of group and almost send me to a colony or prison. My father was furious. I remember speaking with a lawyer and explaining to her what had happened and how. At the time it seemed to me that the police wanted only one thing — money. And in the end, somehow, that was where it all went. I was wrong. I understand that now. Maybe that situation sobered me up. I realised that I could not keep being careless all the time, doing strange things and thinking that I could always get away with it. Sometimes your stupidity can stop being just a funny story and turn into something that can actually break your life. Although I would not say that I used my father’s money as if it were endless. The money was there, but I was given around five thousand hryvnias a month, and I had to manage it wisely. I was not that rich-boy type who spent everything in bars or

restaurants. I always had this thought that if I had money in the future, I could go out into the street and help some homeless person, give him an amount that could help him start a new life. Maybe it sounded naive, but at the time I really thought that way. I always tried to be independent from my father, because I felt that being dependent on someone would not lead to anything good. Money could be nearby, help could be nearby, but inside me there was still this desire to rely only on myself. Not to ask for too much. Not to get used to someone solving things for you. Because if you get too used to another person’s support, later you may not understand how to stand on your own.
