It was winter. After the checkup at the military enlistment office, they diagnosed me with a varicocele — enlarged veins in the scrotum. At school, all boys, I think from around ninth grade, go through a checkup at the military enlistment office. That is how they register us. It was this military building with bars on the windows and doors, with posters about war, about how to assemble a rifle, and different patriotic slogans about the homeland. Some tired flowers in brown pots, long corridors, creaking doors, old stands, the smell of dust, paper, and something hospital-like. Around us were guys in military uniforms, and this place felt not like somewhere you would want to enter, but somewhere you would want to run away from. After that, even school did not seem like such a sad place. On the first floor, there was a room with lamps that flickered a little and reflected off peeling white and green walls. They led us into a small long corridor. At the end of this corridor, there was a window and a pot with some kind of palm tree, like light at the end of the tunnel. There were many doors in this corridor, leading into different offices. Eyesight, hearing, mental health, surgeon, therapist, pediatrician. They examined you completely. They looked into your mouth, at your legs, at your

84 85

back, checked your posture, ears, hair, skin. You had to undress completely in front of your classmates, and some women in white coats touched your body, your genitals, and wrote something down in your file. All of it was very humiliating and strange. After that, they sent us into a room with a psychologist. He asked questions. Who is the president now? What is your relationship with your parents like? Do you use drugs? He asked me to compare myself to some objects. At some point, I do not know why, but I started telling him about how I was being bullied at school. Do you know what happened after that? Exactly. Nothing. He put a little check mark in my file, stamped that I had passed the examination, and after that I stood in an office where they told me, well, we will see you again in two years. My parents found out that I had a varicocele and asked why I had not told them about it. We went to the hospital so I could have surgery. It was a very nice hospital. I was standing in the office when the doctor asked me to lower my pants. He was a little surprised and said that I had large balls. And at that moment I was only thinking about how not to get aroused from him checking them. I was told that I needed surgery. It would take very little time and would be done under anesthesia. That same day, they admitted me to the hospital to prepare me for the operation a couple of days later, after checking the test results. On the day of the surgery, they wheeled me away on a stretcher. I lay there and looked at the ceiling, at the cold light illuminating my face. We went into the elevator, and the sweet nurses kept calming me down. When they brought me into the operating room, everything was so white. Snow was falling outside the window, and it was very cold outside. My mother was supposed to come to me, but because of the weather conditions, she was a little late. They started connecting me to the machines. The doctors’ cold gloves touched my testicles, people were rushing around me. Someone said that I had the pulse of an astronaut. Later, I found out that this meant good indicators, a calm and resilient body. One

nurse inserted a needle and said that I would gradually fall asleep. Before the operation, for some reason, I remembered a video about people who had been given anesthesia, but it had not worked, and they felt the pain of the incision. My body was trembling a little, but I tried to control it. At some point, it was as if I was resisting, but I did not even notice how I sank into sleep. I dreamed of a snowy road. Fast snow. Cars were flying along the highway, yellow headlights shining in the darkness, everything covered in thick fog. The road was very slippery and unsafe. Then I woke up. They told me that everything was over and that everything had gone well. Sleepy after the anesthesia, I saw that cold light again. It seemed to cast shadows on the ceiling. When I woke up already in the ward, my mother was sitting next to me. She said, “Son, I was in a car crash.” She told me that a car coming toward her had swerved into her lane. Mom did not have time to avoid it and jumped out of the car while it was spinning 360 degrees and being thrown into a ditch. The passenger in the car that had driven into her lane died on the spot. Mom told me how his body changed color and how he screamed. She got away with a severe concussion and a slight dislocation of her arm. I remember how easily she could lose consciousness, how she suffered from dizziness and headaches. That same day after the operation, they discharged me. I remember how we sat in a taxi. Mom was crying. We stayed with friends in Zaporizhzhia so that the next day my father could pick us up and take us back to Enerhodar.

You can fall face-first into shit as many times as you need to. You can get up dirty, angry, ridiculous and humiliated, with the feeling that the whole world has seen you like that. The almost eight-hour road seemed to cut my life into two parts. In one part, there remained the house, my bed, the living room, the garden, the green grass under bare feet, and the light smell of blooming sakura that always appeared in the air so quietly, as if someone had opened an invisible window and let calm inside. In the other part, there was Odesa. The city I had chosen myself, although at the time I still did not fully understand what it meant to choose a new life. I sat in the car beside my mother and kept catching myself on the same desire: to turn back. To wake up in the morning in my room, to hear the familiar sounds of the house, the voice of my father, who burst into the room, opened the curtains, turned on the light and music with the words: “Good morning,” to see my friends, to go out into the yard and pretend that there had been no road. That I was not leaving anywhere. That my boxes and suitcases were not lying in the trunk. That I was not sixteen years old and was not going to a city where I would have to study hairdressing, finish school at evening school after classes at the academy, and slowly get used to the thought that from now on I was becoming more responsible for my own life. But the car kept driving. Outside the windows stretched the road, fields, gas stations, gray asphalt softened by heat, and the smell of gasoline. Inside me, fear mixed with some almost painful inspiration. I imagined fashion shows, glossy magazines, incredible haircuts, master classes, my own chain of salons, people who came to me not just for a hairstyle, but for the feeling that they had been seen as beautiful. In my head, all of it already existed: light, mirrors, music, clean work tables, confident movements of hands, applause after a show. And next to it lived another feeling, small and stubborn, like a stone in a shoe. I wanted to go home. Memories came one after another, as if trying to hold me by the sleeve. I looked forward and understood that I

had to take this step, no matter how frightening it was. We arrived at my new apartment, which we had rented from a very sweet woman and her husband. She was a real Odesa woman, with that strict, slightly theatrical way of speaking. The apartment was located at Katerynynska 24. Black iron gates into the courtyard stood between two clothing stores. Outside, the street was noisy with boutiques, shop windows, supermarkets, restaurants with summer terraces, bars, and summer bustle. In summer, it was especially crowded there. A small arch led into a courtyard tightly pressed from all sides by five-story buildings. It was a typical Odesa courtyard, with cats, old balconies, peeling paint, and laundry stretched through the whole space from one window to another. Sheets, towels, T-shirts, and colored pillowcases hung above your head like flags. The buildings stood so close to one another that you could see someone walking through a kitchen, a woman placing a cup on a table, a curtain moving from a hand or a draft. My apartment was on the third floor. A staircase with metal railings and patterned forged elements led to it. Almost every old house in Odesa seemed to keep another city beneath it: catacombs carved in limestone, from which most of old Odesa was built. The apartment had huge ceilings and double doors that opened wide and let daylight into the long corridor. The bedroom was filled with old furniture, patterned paintings, candelabras, a chandelier, and a large bookcase. Two huge windows with wooden frames opened almost full height and made the room even more spacious. Grapes grew outside the windows. They thickly wrapped around the house, stretched along the walls and bars, and clung to the air with their green leaves. When the wind passed through the courtyard, the leaves rustled. The walls were shades of green with a floral pattern. Under my feet lay a soft green carpet. It had that special smell of an old apartment, which I remembered from my grandmother’s house. Through the corridor, you could go into the hall. A large brown chandelier with crystal hung there. There were dark curtains on the

92 93

windows. A wooden balcony faced the courtyard, and through it sounds entered the room: cats meowing, neighbors’ voices, doors slamming, dishes clinking. In the room, there was a television, a large fold-out sofa, several armchairs, and again, a carpet. Everything was a little heavy, old-fashioned. Through double doors, you could step down onto a small step into the kitchen. It was small and compact, with an old gas stove, small storage cabinets, and a small table. There were two doors from it. One led to the bathroom and the other to an additional bedroom. That room was a small extension to the apartment, with two small windows facing an inner courtyard where sunlight almost never reached. Because of that, it was always dark there. There were several wardrobes and an old sofa. Almost nothing else. I made that room into my wardrobe. I walked through the whole apartment and suddenly felt very clearly that in a few days I would stay here alone. My mother would leave, the door would close behind her, and this whole apartment would become not just a place, but a space where I would have to learn to live by myself. My mother helped me clean the apartment, unpack things, go shopping, buy hygiene products and different small items to make this place a little cozier. We folded clothes, wiped surfaces, opened cabinets, checked dishes. I remember the first night especially well. A large moon shone straight into my room. Long greenish curtains slowly moved from the wind. Somewhere far away, a tourist boat gave a long horn. Sometimes it even seemed to me that I could hear waves breaking against the shore, although most likely it was my imagination. I lay in bed and thought about the first day at the academy. My heart was beating too fast. I did not know whether I would manage to do anything at all. Whether I would look ridiculous. Whether everyone would look at me like a child. Whether I would understand on the very first day that I had invented too big a dream for myself. The room was dark, but the moonlight made the outlines of the furniture soft and strange. The bookcase stood against the wall, candelabras

glimmered, grapes moved outside the window in the wind, and everything around me felt not mine. In the morning, I was woken by seagulls or pigeons that landed on the balcony roof and loudly stomped on the metal. My mother was already awake and making breakfast for me. I thought for a long time about what to wear on the first day. Outside, there was warm summer weather. The trees were green and dense. In the courtyard, cats meowed loudly, calling for their owners to bring them food. My mother gave me advice: do not be shy, ask if you do not understand something, be attentive. I listened and nodded, but inside there was still a lump. It was only eight minutes to the academy. We drove down Hretska Street to Hretska 1a, crossed Rishelievska, then Pushkinska, drove over the bridge and crossed Devolanivskyi Descent. It is one of the oldest streets of Odesa. When the car stopped, my palms were damp. I looked at the second floor of the building where the academy was located. Large panoramic windows reflected the street and the sky. Behind the glass, you could see white tile, glossy surfaces, light. The glass door opened almost silently. Inside, there was a reception desk with a glass display case, white pots with large green plants, long glass cabinets with white glossy shelves lit by cold light. Haircare products from T. stood perfectly straight, as if every jar had been placed with a ruler. Two girls in uniform looked very neat. Dark vests, white shirts, gathered hair, minimal makeup. They stood up, smiled, greeted me, and gave me a small tour of the academy. It was small, divided by glass partitions with metal frames. These partitions could be moved to unite the space. Inside, there was also a small salon separated by a glass wall, where students were not allowed to enter. There was a place for belongings, a small break area, the director’s office, and a toilet. The floor was laid with white tile with a black outline around the perimeter. Everywhere there were glass shelves, client chairs, mirrors. Later, I would invite models here for haircuts. But back then, I simply stood in the middle of that academy and felt that

94 95

everyone around me was much older than me. They were about twenty-five and older. I went into the toilet, looked at myself in the mirror, and quietly said that I could do everything. That I should not be afraid. I repeated it again and again, looking at my face, which was trying to seem calm. In the mirror, it was me, but somehow a little different. I fixed my clothes, breathed in, breathed out. The lesson was almost beginning. There were about ten or twelve people in our group. We gathered to introduce ourselves. Everyone said why they wanted to connect their life with hairdressing. I listened and waited for my turn. When it came to me, I said that one day I would have a chain of salons where people could receive a high level of service at an affordable price. I, a sixteen-year-old boy, frightened, tired after the move, missing home and still dreaming of turning back, suddenly said my future out loud. In front of strange adult people. And for a few seconds, that future seemed real. It stood before me as clearly as the light in the panoramic windows of the second floor, and I still did not know how much I would have to lose, confuse, survive, and begin again.

***

I remember the hard days at Tarasyuk school. From morning until evening we learned the basics of hairdressing. We studied shape, lines, partings, elevation angles, trained on models and pretended that all of it could be understood quickly if you just watched the teacher’s hands carefully enough. In reality, at sixteen I was simply standing there with scissors in my hands and trying not to show that inside I was panicking. I remember my first failure very clearly. I cut a model’s hair badly when she came in for a haircut. At least that is how it felt to me then. That evening I was crushed. I walked across the bridge in the cold evening light of office lamps. Around me there were glass windows, cars and the evening air after a whole day spent indoors. I called my mother to tell her about my day. My voice was shaking even though

I tried to speak normally. I was incredibly anxious. Maybe it was not really about the haircut itself. It was more about the feeling that I might not manage at all. That I had come to Odesa, chosen this academy, started a new life and now I was standing on a bridge unable to even cut someone’s hair properly. Fear was taking over also because I was scared of not meeting my father’s expectations. He had already treated my choice with so much skepticism. There was always something heavier in that skepticism than simple doubt. I remember my mother speaking to me in a calm voice: “Listen, these are only your first lessons. This is normal.” And she almost always added my age: “You are only sixteen.” She said it gently. Without pressure. As if she was trying to bring me back into my body, back into reality, back to the fact that I was not supposed to know how to do everything at once. The phone call helped a little, but it still was not the same as coming home. A real home was where there was warm light, the smell of freshly cooked food and my father lying on the huge brown sofa watching a film and shouting from the room: “Son, hi, how was your day?” The key turned twice in the door. The door opened. The long corridor met me with silence and the whole big apartment immediately became too big. I turned on the television just to create some kind of noise. Sometimes I put on headphones and imagined that I was walking down a runway or creating my own show like Victoria’s Secret. In the living room, among the old furniture, the carpet, the dark curtains and the crystal chandelier, I could spin around, walk back and forth and pretend there were lights, cameras, music, voices and applause around me. I was always afraid that the neighbors would see me through the windows or the balcony. That they would see me moving alone in an empty apartment. Although what exactly they could understand from it I did not even know myself. I cooked well. All those years of watching my mother in the kitchen and being curious about it were not wasted. I knew how to cut something, fry it, mix it, how to make normal food out of simple products, how to

96 97

stretch money and not spend everything at once. I was given a small amount of money that I had to make last for a month, and I learned how to count, choose carefully, deny myself things, buy only what I needed and still sometimes take some small treat just to feel that life was something more than saving money and discipline. I always tried to stretch the day as much as possible so I could go to bed as late as I could. I did not want that silence. I did not want to turn off the light. I did not want to stay alone in the apartment. Open windows let in the noise of the city and the distant sounds of the sea. Today is March 9, 2026. Ten years have passed. Stas, you are strong. Truly. Not in the way people usually say it just to cover someone’s pain with a pretty phrase. But in the way that means you lived through all of this and still stayed alive, feeling, attentive, strange, creative and real. Do not listen to anyone who tries to make you smaller. Wipe your tears. You did everything right. Sleep. Tomorrow will be another day.

***

Let me introduce you a little to the city itself, so you can step away from my apartment and the academy and get a better sense of where all of this was happening. Odesa is not a city you can understand at first glance. You have to get used to it. You can get angry at it. You can fall in love with it. You can want to leave a couple of times and still later remember it with tenderness. It has salty skin, sunburned hair, the smell of the sea, coffee, old entrances, fish, hot sand, and cheap perfume from passersby. The main street is considered Deribasivska, but it does not look ceremonial in the usual sense. There is no feeling that the city is trying to impress you. Stone pavement under your feet, trees along the street, many cafés and shops, street musicians, a small fair, old people on benches, people walking slowly as if they have no important business for the day. The houses on Deribasivska are low, old, with add-ons and air conditioners in the windows. They do not have that

artificial pomp where a place seems to have been made especially for tourist photographs. There is more of a feeling of real life there. Nearby is the City Garden. Many trees, leaves above your head creating shadows, benches, a small square with a gazebo where street musicians could play by evening. Near Deribasivska and the City Garden stands the Opera Theater, pompous, with stucco, rounded forms, a heavy facade, statues, arches, carriages with horses, and dressed-up people by evening. The fountains splash water. Evening light glints on dresses with rhinestones. Farther on, the city descends toward Prymorskyi Boulevard. It is a spacious boulevard with a view of the port, water, ships, the horizon, trees along the alleys, and the abandoned hotel on the pier named “Odesa.” In winter, the trees on the boulevard are decorated with garlands, and they create the effect of a portal because they glow one after another, as if you are walking not simply along an alley, but through some corridor from the past into the present. There on the boulevard is also a glass dome with the remains of archaeological excavations of old Odesa. At the beginning of the boulevard stands the monument to Pushkin, sometimes painted with spray paint, and there is a story behind that. After the full-scale war, many Russian names, monuments, streets, documents, school teaching, language, and cultural symbols in Ukraine began to be reconsidered. Somewhere this is called Ukrainianization, somewhere decolonization, somewhere derussification. The point is that the country began very sharply to return to itself its names, its language, its memory, and its meanings, because for too long Ukrainian history, culture, and the right to be a separate country had been suppressed or pushed into the background. Especially after the Russian invasion, it became impossible to pretend that all these monuments and names were simply standing in the city neutrally, like decoration. So streets are renamed, Russian and Soviet monuments are removed or discussed, figures like Lenin have long been taken down, and people often divide into two camps. For

98 99

Odesa this is especially sensitive because the city has always been mixed, complex, port-like, and multilingual. Before the Russian Empire, this place was Hadjibey, a Tatar-Ottoman settlement and fortress. Then the territory came under the control of the Russian Empire, and at the end of the eighteenth century a port began to be developed here, which later became Odesa. In the nineteenth century, the city was an important Black Sea port of the empire, but that does not mean it was simply a “Russian city.” It was always a mixture: Ukrainians, Jews, Greeks, Bulgarians, Moldovans, Russians, French, Italians, Germans. A kind of port Babylon where everyone brought their own language, goods, habits. After 1917, Odesa passed from hand to hand, and different forces fought for it. Later, it became part of Soviet Ukraine, and in 1991, together with Ukraine, it became part of an independent state. And an important point: Odesa region also voted for Ukraine’s independence. Near the boulevard is the city hall. Below it is Istanbul Park, and a little farther, Greek Park. Then the Potemkin Stairs. It has ten flights and almost two hundred steps. If you look from below, then at the top stands Duke de Richelieu, a French aristocrat who governed Odesa at the beginning of the nineteenth century and strongly influenced its development as a port European city. If you walk farther from the monument to the end of the boulevard, you will find the Vorontsov Colonnade. It stands above the slope against the background of the port and the city. It was built in the nineteenth century as part of the Vorontsov Palace. A little farther, if you move away from the boulevard, Odesa becomes even more chaotic. Arches, courtyards, old entrances, peeling walls, ropes with laundry, balconies with wrought iron, windows behind which someone is frying fish, someone is arguing in Odesa slang, someone is listening to the radio or chanson on the balcony, someone has lived there for so many years that, as people say, he is an Odesan in the fifth generation and knows neighbors by their footsteps. If you enter almost any Odesa courtyard,

especially in the old district, there will always be wet laundry, cats, someone else’s dishes on tables, neighbors who can eat together right in the courtyard, the smell of food, peeling creaking doors, rusty railings, and some voices from apartments above. After Deribasivska, one of the most important places for the city is Pryvoz. Pryvoz is a market. It is the heart of the city, where you can buy fresh fish, greens, fruit, spices, pickles, cheese. It is plastic bags, old scales, bargaining, jokes, insults, fights, theft, laughter, and smells that hit your nose immediately. As I wrote earlier, I often explored Odesa by bicycle, and once I went to Moldavanka. This is a completely different Odesa. Low houses, very old facades, dusty streets, small passages, courtyards inside courtyards. Simple life, a little poor, very human. On my bicycle, I often went down to Lanzheron, then farther along the shore, where there can be incredible sunsets and sunrises, where people slowly go down to the sea and the air smells of warm stone, seaweed, and corn. French Boulevard, where I later moved from Prymorskyi district to the Arcadia area, has old estates and sanatoriums. One of the estates was turned into a restaurant well-known in Odesa called “Dacha.” There is also Soborna Square, which I have already written about before. There you can often meet old men who come to play checkers and chess. On the same square stands the Spaso-Preobrazhenskyi Cathedral, where in summer, during the heat, I could go in just to sit among white stone, under huge icons in golden frames, in the coolness. Odesa is laundry on the balcony. Catacombs under old houses. The smell of the sea and seaweed. Fresh fish in restaurants. The old tram that goes along French Boulevard and through Pryvoz. A cat on hot stone. Seagulls under the windows. Gossip in my barber chair and the eternal question: “Are you from Odesa?” A woman with a bag of vegetables from Pryvoz. A man without a shirt on a balcony with a radio. Tourists. Cruise ships in the port.

100 101

***

There has always been this strange feeling of trust in people inside me. I do not know how to name it correctly. Naivety? Rose-colored glasses? Stupidity? Or simply a desire to believe that the person in front of you will not hurt you on purpose. I opened up quickly. It seemed to me that people also stood in front of me without armor and without weapons. But then those sweet smiles could whisper your name somewhere between your failures. And I had no armor against those smirks, those little jokes. I did not know how to pretend that I did not care. Sometimes I think about homeless people. Do they pay attention to how people treat them? Or at some point is a person forced to build such armor around themselves that other people’s gazes simply pass through them? When I walked past people like that, I often thought that I would want to help them if I ever had enough money. It seemed to me that maybe some of them simply could not build that armor inside themselves. Could not become rude, arrogant, closed. Could not withstand a world that constantly demands you to be stronger than you are. And what even is that inner core inside you? Being arrogant? Stubborn? Not asking for anything? Not crying? Not showing that you are hurt? I still cannot answer this question. But I definitely do not like it when people whisper behind my back. And maybe the worst thing is that every time, I still want to believe people again.

***

My birthday. We gathered in a beautiful restaurant. I celebrated most of my birthdays with my parents, and the older I became, the more special that moment felt to me. With age you begin to understand that things like this may never happen again. That a family sitting at one table, even when everything looks ordinary, is not really such an ordinary thing. But I could hardly call my nineteenth birthday joyful. All evening there were little

digs between my mother and my father. I could see that my mother was clearly upset with him about something. In our family back then we did not really talk about problems. At least not out loud. Everyone could feel that something was happening, but no one asked directly. And I also could not ask, “What is going on with you?” My mother was wearing a stunning long black lace dress. Long hair, red lips, diamonds in her ears. She looked very beautiful, but there was tension in her. My father, as always, was dressed in his strict style: a polo shirt, trousers, shoes. My brother spent the whole evening on his phone, playing games, which was quite typical of him. They brought us beautiful desserts. Very beautiful. The kind that should have made the evening a little softer, but they softened nothing. Not between my mother and father, and not inside me. My father had booked a hotel room directly above the restaurant. Apparently, it was supposed to be the continuation of the evening. But my mother had a breakdown and refused to stay there. We left in a taxi. I sat inside that car and felt the celebration finally collapse somewhere downward. Street lights in the window, the air inside the car was stuffy. When we arrived at the apartment on Katerynynska Street, they started shouting at each other. At some point my father came up to me, kissed me on the head and said, “Goodbye, son.” Then he left. I stayed with my mother and my brother. My mother was in some state I could not read. She was rushing around, angry, crying or almost crying, and then she went after him. I did not understand what was worrying and angering her so much that she was losing control like that. I did not understand why my father had said that to me. He had never done anything like that before. But there were often scandals in my family. There were fights too. I found drops of blood on the floor. I saw my mother covered in bruises. I saw cuts on my father’s hands. Then everyone could pretend that life simply went on.

102 103

***

Rolling down Bunina Street on my bicycle and crossing the avenues, I saw how the orange streetlights cut into my shadow. I raced without stopping at red lights, straight to Kotsebu Bridge, and then farther toward Shevchenko Park. The bike lanes led to Lanzheron, and from there Trassa Zdorovya stretched along the beaches and the shore all the way to Arkadia. There was almost no space on that road, but Zemfira was playing in my headphones, and I was full of energy and some light, rightful revenge inside myself. I did not stop, and it felt as if I was gaining an unbearably huge speed. People and trees around me turned into lines, into blurred particles of movement, and for a few minutes the city stopped being a city and became a flow. This was my most ordinary March. Every evening after school, I rode here to pour out my emotions and not stay alone in the apartment with my fantasies. I reached one very important place. There was a bench and an acacia tree on the slope, from where the whole coast of Odesa and the moon opened in front of me. I sat there and watched how its light fell on the surface of the water. What was beyond that horizon? Was I successful? Was I proud of myself? No. I did not think about that. I was more likely giving thanks and asking for a little. Asking for strength. Asking for a sign. Asking for all this movement to lead me somewhere. Then I breathed out and rode on. Almost to Arkadia, bright and full of lights. But this brightness was not soft or beautiful. It was sticky, aggressive, and almost vulgar. After the dark tunnel of trees on Trassa Zdorovya, Arkadia appeared like a foreign set: clubs, signs, flashes of light, glass facades, loud music, security at the entrances, girls in heels and dresses that were too short, with heavy makeup and phones in their hands. Boys in tight T-shirts with pumped arms, watches, cars, expensive perfume mixed with the smell of hookah, alcohol, fried food, and the

sea. Everything there seemed to be trying to prove that it lived better than it really did. VIP tables, bottles, hookahs, ice buckets, camera flashes, poses for Instagram, faces that held the expression of happiness for too long. People stood at the entrances to clubs under neon, trying to catch an angle where their life would look more expensive. There was something funny and sad in it at the same time. Everyone seemed to be taking part in one big performance about success, body, money, and freedom, but there was almost no freedom in it. What I felt more was the exhaustion of needing to be desired and rich. Arkadia was like a phone screen enlarged to the size of a district: bright, noisy, glossy, filtered, broken glasses, girls fixing their makeup in the reflection of black glass. I rode past on my worn-out bicycle in an oversized gray sweater and felt both foreign and not foreign at the same time. Past tall buildings, past several skyscrapers with orange lighting, along the smooth paved road on Prospekt Shevchenka, through Park Pobedy, and out toward Odesa’s main railway station, where people buried in poverty and problems were trying to climb out. In the end, I turned onto my street, Ekaterininskaya. And so it went every other day, almost every night. I came home, took a shower, and lay down in bed, listening to the quiet sound of the courtyard.

***

Grandmother L. came to visit me in Odesa. She got off the bus tired and said that she had been feeling nauseous the whole way. She always had a problem with that. It was already evening when we were riding in a taxi through the streets of Odesa. I could not believe that she was with me. I was looking forward to showing her Odesa. She had not been to the sea for a long time, and the last trip of hers that I really remember was to Crimea with a friend, on a voucher given to workers of the nuclear power plant. Although she did not work at the plant, so I still do not fully understand what kind of voucher she actually used to go there. When we pulled up

104 105

to my archway with the gate, we got out of the taxi. Shop windows lit the street, live music came from the cafés and restaurants, the street was busy, and we walked around people to get inside. Grandmother asked many questions. She leaned on the railing as we climbed to the second floor of my apartment. I had already prepared a bed for her in my bedroom, and I settled in the farthest room of the apartment, where in the morning the light almost never enters and it is always dark. I tried to give her the brightest moments. To go to a restaurant or drink a cappuccino, which she had never tried before. I took her to my academy to dye her hair. My teachers stood with color samples, and using a special formula, we chose a shade that could cover her gray hair. I felt some kind of mockery around us. As if my real connection with my grandmother was being disturbed by some stupid looks. Almost eight years later, she still remembers how delicately I applied the dye to her head. She lay with me on the beach, threw stones into the sea, and slightly lowered her feet into the cold water, giving herself a massage by stepping in place on the stones. In the evenings, she rubbed my hands with a special ointment called Zvezdochka. It smelled of something minty and had always been a universal remedy for headaches, flu, and muscle pain. We drank tea with cheese and talked until late at night, as we always did, as if not breaking our tradition.

***

The sun shone through the car window, onto my face, my hands, and the ruts. It was hot inside, the trunk was full of bags filled with groceries from shopping and a walk by the sea, and everything seemed to be going well. We were driving together: me, my brother, my mom, and my dad. We had plans to go out to dinner that evening. My mom suddenly asked me whether I used condoms when I had sex with girls. I immediately became embarrassed. Not because the question was scary, but because it had nothing to do with me. I had never had sex with girls.

I don’t think I even had the words yet to explain what was going on inside me. I couldn’t say, “Mom, I’m not talking about girls.” I couldn’t say, “I don’t understand it myself yet.” I couldn’t say anything honest. I mumbled something. I don’t remember what exactly. It must have been something neutral and safe, some sound instead of an answer, a teenage attempt to disappear while remaining in the backseat of the car. And then my father abruptly turned to me from the front seat. His voice became harsh, as if my mother’s question wasn’t a question, but a red button or a trigger that was already in his head. He yelled, “Or are you into boys, huh?” I remember him looking at me as if he was trying to catch me in the act. As if I had already done something. As if my face and my embarrassment were already proof. I didn’t have time to say anything. He continued speaking harshly and louder. “If I ever find out that you’re a faggot, you’ll go home and work as a loader for me,” he said. Then he started talking about the dignity of family. About shame. About how people will point fingers. About gossip around him and our family. Faggot. The word hung in the car, very dirty and very loud. My mother didn’t stop him. The car kept going, the sun kept streaming in, the day outside remained as bright as if nothing had happened. When the car stopped at a red light, I was barely holding back the tears. They were close, in my eyes, in my throat, on my face, but I tried to hold them back. Crying in front of them would have been further proof. Of weakness, guilt, wrongdoing, anything. In moments like these, even pain can’t be shown normally, because it can immediately be used against you. I opened the car door and got out. No, I ran out. I walked down the street and held back the tears.

***

Still, there were moments when I was happy that my parents came to visit me. They did not always know how to react to things in the right way. I am sure they suspected something about me. And I am especially sure

106 107

that my mother felt it. I will not pretend it was not there: they even discussed it with my father and thought about finding me a psychologist. My mother told me this much later, when I had already grown up. I loved my mother in my own way and I loved my father in my own way too. They were just different languages of love, and we did not always understand each other. They came together, sometimes separately, and I felt so sad when they left. The apartment became too big for me again. On the day of their departure there was such a lump in my throat that sometimes it was hard to breathe. I held back my tears while sitting in the car, then came home and cried alone because there no one could see me. I remember how my father bought me razor blades. He gave them to me, and I secretly left them in his car so I would not have to show that I needed them. For a long time I pretended that hair did not grow on my body. For some reason I was ashamed of the hair on my face and body. I always shaved it, but hid it from my parents, as if there was something shameful about it. In general I had a lot of complexes about my body. At the beach I always lay in a T-shirt and did not want to take it off in front of my parents. It was as if I was hiding myself all the time, even in the most ordinary things. And with my mother it was strange too. I could not always show love to her openly. I did not kiss her for no reason, I felt shy about hugging her, shy about lying next to her on the bed. I always sat on the edge, as if there had to be some safe distance between us. But on birthdays or Mother’s Day I could calmly hug her and kiss her because those gestures had a reason.

***

You know I was almost finished with Tarasyuk School of Hairdressing and all we had left was the exam. We had to show the skills we had been taught all that time: shape, lines, styling, haircuts and confidence. I had almost none of that confidence back then but I still had to pretend it was there. I remember inviting my friend

N. to be my model for the exam but she was very nervous about her hair and ended up leaving. So I was left without a model but somehow I managed to find another one and pass. It was still hard for me and despite my creative behavior, my fantasies, my way of seeing things and my desire to find something special in everything I probably still lacked what the older people around me had. Not even talent. More like some inner structure, stability and an understanding of how to behave in reality when everything does not go as beautifully as it does in your head. In some strange way I got into a salon where you could do an internship through the academy. The salon had the same name as the school. I kept failing and at some point the director of the school told my mother that I should think about changing professions. It hurt to hear that from my mother and it hurt even more to think how hard it must have been for her to hear it herself because she had persuaded my father so much, defended my choice so much and told him that I liked it. And I really did like it. My fantasies were just very far from the reality I faced every day. In my head there were shows, magazines and people thanking you for making them more beautiful. In reality there were uneven cuts, fear, empty appointments, my confusion and the feeling that I was failing again. I took breaks, stayed in Enerhodar and pretended that everything was fine while inside I understood that I was wasting time. I did not want to show my failures to anyone and created the illusion that the cards were still on my side. I guess I simply did not want to look weak. At some point I realized that I could no longer sit around and do nothing. There were many attempts to get into different salons, empty schedules and that strange depressive feeling of places where people live from salary to salary and everything feels simple, closed in and a little airless. As if the system pulls you in and you do not even notice how you become part of it. You start thinking that this is how it is supposed to be: here is your chair, here is the mirror, here is the owner cutting her godmother’s hair, here is

108 109

the administrator telling endless stories about how she went to the market, here the day has passed and here the next one will be exactly the same. I sat in those salons and tried to understand how to get out of it. I remember one salon where I met a very talented cosmetologist. She was incredibly open and her laugh seemed to protect the space around her. Her whole body seemed to know how to hold boundaries. She was always well-groomed with smooth hair tied back in a ponytail. There was something in her voice, in the way she spoke, in the way she moved and looked at people that made me feel lighter. I felt that I could learn a lot from her. She seemed well read, grown and free inside herself. I wanted to listen to her, go into her thoughts, simply be near her and absorb something. But people like that often come into your life like a gift. They teach you a little and then suddenly disappear. At some point all of this started eating me from the inside again and turned into anger and a desire to prove at least something. One day I came across the profile of a guy I had studied with at Tarasyuk school. He had become a barber. At that time almost nobody in Ukraine really understood what a barbershop was but for some reason I decided that I had to try and retrain as a men’s hairdresser. I started looking for a school where they taught fades, clipper work, beard shaving and head shaving. A new desire woke up in me. It was as if my eyes opened again. I started watching more videos, studying technique, clipper work and the shape of the male head. I found a school that offered training, took the money I had asked my mother for and started courses in one barbershop where they promised to teach me and give me a job after the training. Everything was new to me. They used straight razors, placed hot towels on the face to steam the skin before shaving and sprayed special cologne. Typical salon interiors suddenly turned into leather sofas, magazines with girls, an administrator offering clients whiskey, beer in the fridge, football or boxing on the TV and rough-looking male barbers around me cutting the hair of other men like them. And that was

when I first touched a man’s head so closely. I could feel its shape and not show that I was feeling something while I was lathering his hair. I could touch him so close, touch his neck, his ears and his hairline. It was a strange first feeling. Washing a guy’s hair and combing it. I felt as if I was dominating a little. As if I was controlling his head. Our faces were very close and all of it was supposedly happening within the training but inside me something still tightened and moved too fast. But it did not last long because my fade was not good enough. The transitions were dirty and the cutting lines looked bad. The training ended halfway through. They returned my money and said: “Sorry but we cannot teach you.” What do you think it feels like to hear that for the second time? Do you think I took that money and calmly went to another salon or barbershop to ask them to teach me again? No, my hands just dropped. I was tired and standing on the bridge not far from Tarasyuk school and Hretska Street with my phone in my hand. I was about to call my mother and tell her that I had failed again. She did not shout and she did not sound upset. She only asked if they had returned my money and said that maybe I should go home and rest after a day like that. I hung up and walked toward the bus stop where the bus was supposed to take me back to my neighborhood. I opened Google Maps but not to build a route home. I opened it to look at barbershops nearby. Apparently even when I was completely broken some part of me still refused to give up. I chose one barbershop by its pictures and by the interior I liked. It was inside an old building in the city center, one of those places that seemed to belong to another time. The entrance led into a covered courtyard with worn tiles underfoot, a pale glass ceiling above, dark wooden frames, old arches and small shops on the lower floor. The place had once probably been something more elegant, maybe a hotel or a trading house. I walked into that barbershop and asked if they needed barbers and whether they trained people. On that same day, I had been kicked out of training. The administrator asked how

110 111

old I was. I remember lying and saying that I was older than I actually was just to get the job. A barber came up to me, put his hand on my shoulder and said he would teach me. I gave him the money. And that is how the most successful part of my hairdressing story began.

***

It turns out that things like harmony, simplicity and friendliness can quietly change your inner state. You start feeling that you can actually do things. You stop waiting for a mistake all the time. People treat you with respect and explain things calmly as if they do not want to break this fragile state. Suddenly you begin to understand everything very quickly. Real professionals worked there. People with precise movements, confident hands, a light scent of cologne and a calm focus that I lacked so much at the time. In some almost miraculous way I ended up there with no experience and after just a couple of weeks of training I began taking clients. Before I started working they still found out my real age and sometimes I think about what would have happened if I had told the truth right away. That thin borderline and that risk somehow saved me then and gave me a chance. Behind the bar counter I met N. There was so much complexity in her that it seemed she could change the space around her just by being there. She easily played with any scene, pulled hidden meanings out of ordinary things, turned people a little inside out and showed them differently as if she already knew their weak spots. She was the leader inside the male team but without rough pressure. You could feel it through her calm confidence. She easily found a common language with people. She could flirt, intrigue and joke but there was always a clear boundary in her eyes that nobody crossed. Sometimes one look from her was enough to understand her. When she walked into the barbershop I always lifted my head to see what she was wearing that day. Her style was an extension of herself. It never looked like an outfit made just to impress. We slowly got used to each

other and asked simple questions but behind them there was always something more: the desire to understand who we were to each other, where we crossed, where we separated and what distance we could keep. I felt a distance between us. Not physical but internal. Like a difference in depth. I tried to build a bridge, to come closer to her perception and to catch up with the way she saw the world. With her I began noticing things that had passed me by before: the texture of objects, different angles of perception, pauses in conversation and the mood of a space. I started thinking differently about relationships, closeness, friendship and flirting. Her hair often fell onto her face when she was booking a haircut. Soft strands touched her cheeks and she did not move them away right away. Clear speech, a calm voice, a smile and subtle well-timed jokes made almost every man who entered the barbershop feel comfortable. She noticed everything: uneven light, an unnecessary object, a person’s mood, a desire they had not yet managed to say out loud. If I had to describe her through music I would think of Tame Impala, La Femme and probably the soundtrack to Twin Peaks. Something slightly foggy, hypnotic, with depth and a little anxiety. I felt a little nervous around her. But it was she who seemed to push me deeper into this new world where there was more taste, more observation and some kind of grown-up intelligence. A world where I suddenly felt that I was in the right place. As if beside her I started looking at myself from another side.

***

I had never felt anything like that before. I was nineteen and I still had not tried sex, but I was slowly starting to accept certain things in myself that I had suppressed before and never explored as deeply back in Enerhodar. I was growing up and becoming more confident in my interests. Or maybe it only seemed that way to me. Probably the first attraction I truly felt was toward a guy who worked with me at the salon. He was older than

112 113

me, not tall and not short, with long thick fingers and wide forearms, a slightly elongated face, scars on his skin, a bit of stubble and expressive lips. He was not skinny and not full. I often watched him cut hair. I watched how his hands moved, how his fingers worked, how his face changed, how he slightly pressed his lips together when he was focused. His speech was tactful and structured. As if he always weighed everything on a scale and kept two possible answers inside him. Maybe that is what people call being reasonable. It seemed to me that he almost always won every argument or conversation that came up among friends over a glass of beer in a local bar. I never drank alcohol with my colleagues and I never went out for smoke breaks. Those habits of alcohol and cigarettes somehow passed me by. His clothes were simple. A basic T-shirt and denim shorts in summer or jeans in winter. At first glance there was nothing especially striking about him. In the beginning, when I had just started working there, it seemed to me that we could have nothing in common, but somehow with time I felt something vulnerable inside myself around him and I started trying to make him like me. I felt something I had never felt before and for the first time I found a male friend. Before that my friends had mostly been girls. In general I had never found a common language with boys at school. I think there was too much difference between us and maybe I was too complicated for them. But I was never rude to my male classmates. We were just always on different wavelengths. With him something inside me began to stretch deeper and open my feelings. For the first time I caught myself thinking that I wanted intimacy with a man. I had never gone on dates, never used dating apps, I just went into work and gave all my time to it. I started studying haircuts more deeply, created an Instagram account, shared my work and different barbers from different cities of Ukraine began following me. I was too strange even for barbers. The haircuts I made, the shoots with models after work, all that way of presenting things, it was not something

ordinary. But in reality that was how I stood apart from most people and found my own handwriting. So to cover the silence and loneliness that had been hanging over me for so long, it seemed to me that going completely into work was the best way. It was easier that way. I was not left alone with my thoughts, with painful memories, with the loneliness that sometimes covered me like cold sea air coming through an open window. He was the only person I trusted to cut my hair. We experimented with my haircut, stayed after closing and talked about everything and nothing. He was one of the first people who taught me how to hold a clipper. He would take my hand and show me how to move it along the head while standing behind my back. It was a strange feeling of such close contact, when our hands touched and I could feel his chest against my back. I wanted him to wash my hair for longer, to run his fingers over my scalp, to pull the wet strands and make the cut. I am not sure whether he felt anything from me, but for a short time we became friends. We went to cafés after work and I always waited for those moments. If he had other plans, I felt disappointed, although I pretended everything was normal. I think at some point I crossed a line and started touching him more often, which probably caused strange looks from the other employees. Sometimes we walked the same way toward his home through evening Odesa. Some streets were not lit at all and if they were lit, it was with a yelloworange light. I remember once asking him to hit me. I shouted: “Hit me. I want you to hit me.” And he did it. A short slap. The hit was not strong, but what was I trying to get from that act? A special moment? A connection? I think I did not want pain, but a controlled collision with an unavailable male force. Through that slap I could receive physical contact, proof of his presence, emotional release and some symbolic punishment for a desire that felt impossible or shameful. That is how I would formulate it now. Sometimes it seemed to me that he also felt something. Maybe he found in me something he did not allow himself to show with others, but he still

114 115

did not let me come any closer. Once he stayed at my place. By then I had already moved into my new apartment in Arcadia, closer to those plastic people, but already with a view of the sea. There it was no longer my fantasy that I could hear the waves. They really filled the room. The apartment had two rooms with big beds and a living room with a sofa. We watched a film and fell asleep. I was drawn to him and our legs kept catching on each other. At some point he asked: “Do you want me to fuck you?” I smiled somehow, got confused and said, “No.” Nothing strange happened after that. We had breakfast, but it seemed like we both moved slightly away from each other. I felt ashamed and disgusted with myself because I had directed my attention toward him instead of work and my career. As if the interest suddenly disappeared and a question appeared inside me: “What are you doing, Stas? This is not your goal.” From paycheck to paycheck I bought foreign currency, came home, counted the money and saved it, economizing more and more. Then he moved to the new branch that our salon opened in my district. We began seeing much less of each other. Sometimes he told me he had a girlfriend, or that he was going on dates.

***

I got an apartment after a year of working in the old branch in the city center. I moved from Katerynynska Street to a district called Arcadia. The same district of Odesa where I once loved riding my bike in my huge gray knitted sweater past girls in Paco Rabanne dresses, neon signs, the smell of vanilla ice cream, tasteless music and guys with Gucci bags across their shoulders. Arcadia is a district, but its whole heart was concentrated on that one alley with restaurants, a water park and a club called Ibiza. Above it there were new apartment blocks and each building was called a Zhemchuzhyna with its own number. After some time our second salon branch opened there and later I was transferred there from the center. The old branch was near Derybasivska and not far

from Soborna Square, where the Spaso-Preobrazhenskyi Cathedral stood. I often went there just to sit in silence. It seemed to me that it was a place where I could ask for something and say thank you. It was always cool there, even in summer, because of the cold marble. When I was transferred to the artificial district of Arcadia, I lost some of my clients. For some people it was only convenient to come to the center, and some simply did not like that district in Odesa because of its unnatural behavior and because it did not feel like the city. The new branch was much bigger. There was a large academy for training, a spacious room and seven workstations. It all sounded cool, but that space did not have the feeling that the old place had. Concrete walls, a new floor and new design could not replace the old room with stone walls and switches, where maybe twentyfive years earlier there had been a small shop selling gloves, hats or something else. Nothing could replace the marble floor under my feet, the huge carved shop windows, stained glass, mirror inserts on the walls, the glass floor and the figures on the walls with angels, half-naked young men and women. Nothing could replace the moment when you leave work and step out onto the main street of Odesa, onto Derybasivska, with its large square, fountains, old facades, stucco, curls and flowers on them. Nothing could replace my marshrutka. That is what yellow buses are called there, where you pay after getting off, shouting to the driver: “Stop here.” Then you pass the money through people to the driver, and the passenger sitting next to him can just throw the banknote for the ride. Nothing could replace the music in my headphones and the summer wind that came into the marshrutka through the open window and slightly moved the curtain. I sat there in my headphones, listening to Crystal Castles, going through my tips in my hands and writing down the final income in my notes after the shift. Nothing could replace the way I gave half of my salary to the currency exchange to get dollars and put them aside for my future. The same future for

116 117

which I once rode my bike from Katerynynska along Trasa Zdorovia to the bench with the tree on the cliff. Now I only had to walk down from my apartment in Arcadia. Ten minutes on foot and I was already close to that place. In summer I usually walked down the slope to cross the whole beach. During the day there were too many people and too many children. But after work, in the evening, when the sun was almost going down behind the horizon and everything around became pink-red, there were fewer people. I jumped from the pier and let the water take me down to the very bottom. When I touched the bottom made of clean sand, I felt that I was good there and anxious at the same time. Around me there was only sand and nothing else. It was as if I was lying there and waiting for something to grab me. And as if I was ready for it. Then the fear passed through me. My body relaxed, my arms became light, and I was no longer fully controlling myself. I opened my eyes underwater, saw the light above, pushed myself off the bottom and floated back up. The warm water touched my face. Then I lay on my back, looked at the sunset and the waves rocked me slightly. I was always close with water, but never with people.

***

N. and I became even closer. We loved doing photoshoots before my breaks between clients. She would show me what she had bought or what painting she had made. She liked photographing her outfits, and then in VSCO we would spend hours choosing the right filter and color correction. She introduced me to her husband, V. Sometimes he came to our salon and waited for N. until she closed the shift, the cash register and the salon itself. V. had a wide neck, ears that were neither big nor small, a rough nose, sharp cheekbones, veins on his hands and strong legs. When he smiled, folds appeared at the corners of his mouth, and he started to look a little like a demon. There was a certain hardness in him, but not in a physical way. More like if a tank ran

over you and you somehow stayed alive. He dressed well. I think it was because of N, because she had given him a sense of style. Something in the spirit of Hedi Slimane and Margiela: long loose T-shirts made of light fabrics, some kind of shorts, vintage shoes, a leather jacket with a long collar, rings on his fingers and a piercing in his nose. When he came to the salon, he usually sat in the leather chair or by the window with his small laptop and did not really draw attention to himself. I did not always even notice him. He seemed to dissolve into the space. Sometimes we played Mortal Kombat on PlayStation, and when he beat me, he smiled with his demonic smile, and his eyes seemed to start shining. V. had medium-length hair and a short fringe. The sides and the back were a little shorter. He styled his hair with matte paste and made it look chaotic. I remember how during the haircut we talked about whether it was possible to disappear from the world but still continue to exist in it. It was night after the salon had closed. After the haircut I took a few photographs of him, drew different hieroglyphs on his face and shot him against a black background. What did I feel for him? If I had known him better, would I still have been drawn to him in the same way? He was definitely beautiful, but was it only beauty? Maybe I was fascinated by them as a couple. He is still stuck in my head to this day. Maybe it was my naivety and my tendency to fall for people around whom I feel safe. Maybe it was not even love from one guy to another. Later, when I was already working in Arcadia, I remember N. and V. came with their dog, A, and after work we walked through Arcadia to the beach. We sat on the sand, looked at the moon and listened to the waves. It was before their trip to South America.

***

When I had money, I was able to travel with my brother I. It was my first trip to Europe, not counting Greece, where I had once spent a couple of weeks with my parents, staying in a huge hotel. But this was already our first

118 119

trip with my brother without our parents. We stayed in a hostel not far from the Heineken factory. It was September, and in the morning there was an incredibly thick fog. The piers, the water, the boats, the houses, everything dissolved in it. A light sun was breaking through that white haze. Cute tilted houses, windows without curtains on the ground floor, trash near the steps, crowds of bicycles on separate bike lanes, already rushing somewhere on their own business and ringing their bells to move people out of the way. Amsterdam was magical in that fog, but then it disappeared quickly. Some trees were still green, and the sun was still warm. We took the elevator up to the roof of a tall building, and my brother, swinging on the swing, was hanging over the drop. From that tower you could see the whole city, as if it had been built in circles. The central streets were packed with tourists, and we tried to move farther away, into smaller streets and alleys. My brother hated me for making us walk for so long, but I always have this desire to see as much as possible. I am pulled toward something new, when after every corner it feels like something else will open up again. And the city really kept changing all the time. As if it was transforming by itself, generating itself again. Of course there was the Red Light District and the girls behind glass, the smell of beer, piss and tobacco. We looked at them, and one girl even tried to lure me in. We bought a big piece of cheese and sat on the pier, watching a boat pass along the canal while the lights on the bridge lit the way for the captain. In that short amount of time we also managed to visit a small village with a lighthouse and cows. And on the way by bus we stopped in Rotterdam. At the time that city seemed to me like a developer’s joke, because everything there felt as if it made no sense. The houses, traffic lights, lamps, street structures, everything had strange forms. The famous barbershop Schorem is located there, the place where many basic foundational haircuts came from, the ones barbers later started using all over the world. Men worked there in a classic style,

in jackets and trousers, in white shirts, with huge moustaches styled with wax. They clicked straight razors, wiped foam from faces, offered beer, and when the old cash register opened, it made that exact sound that immediately reminded you of money: “ching.”

***

One day a woman came into the barbershop. It did not happen often, but sometimes women still asked for the kind of haircut that men usually got with us. Sometimes they came into our salon and said that women’s salons could not cut hair the way men’s salons did. During working hours we were not allowed to take women for haircuts, but after the shift we could voluntarily stay, cut their hair and keep the money for ourselves. For me it was quite good. I often did that because I had some basic knowledge of how to cut women’s hair, and in general I was interested in experimenting. It could also be good for my portfolio. So most of the time I said yes. And then one grown woman, about forty-five, stayed after the shift and sat in my typical barber’s leather and metal chair with a footrest. She said she needed to cut her hair because soon she was going to start chemotherapy. She had a cancerous tumor, and knowing that she would lose her hair, she wanted to make it shorter in advance. She asked me to shave the sides. She was very cheerful. Her voice sank into me and seemed to catch on every part inside me. A joyful voice, but almost on the edge of crying. That made it slightly hoarse. She told me old stories about Odesa, some criminal things about the famous Pryvoz market, about her family, her life, her work and her diagnosis. You know, in three years of working there, a huge number of people passed through me, and with many of them I had to be something like a psychologist or a therapist. At such a young age I felt so many other people’s problems and heard so many tragic stories about love, life, work, money, children, wives, debts and deaths, that I carried all that weight on myself afterwards. I waited for the moment when I

120 121

could dive into the sea or stand under a hot shower. I was like a filter. Like a gate of cleansing. They talked everything out, and I cut some kind of weight from their shoulders and helped them feel a little better. Sometimes it seemed to me that they were taking my youth from me and that I was getting old too early. I was like a guide. After our small ritual they thanked me, I hugged them, and they left. Some never came back, and some came again and again. I saw them in different moods, in different events, in different periods of life. Over time I became almost a part of their family. We congratulated each other on holidays and gave each other small gifts. I will say that specific clients always found me. People who were on the same wavelength as me. As if we had all accidentally landed on planet Earth and were trying to settle here somehow. I always felt my clients, and it was immediately clear through the energy between us. I cut that woman’s hair. I remember how she sat there in glasses and almost cried. We were alone in the barbershop. It was dark outside the window. There was silence between us. For me it was still too heavy. I did not fully understand that I was really helping her. I was just doing what I knew how to do. I remember that we hugged. I remember that she came to me a couple more times to even out the haircut. And then I never saw her again. I hope you beat that illness.

***

Returning to my city Enerhodar by bus took around ten hours. Usually it happened before my birthday, before my parents’ birthdays or around holidays like New Year. Sometimes it could happen in summer too, but not often. I got off the bus with a different feeling toward everything I saw. Although when I lived in that city I understood that it was not perfect. It was a kind of routine utopia that could easily swallow you like a whirlpool if you did not leave in time. Young people did not stay there. The blue buses for the nuclear power plant and the yellow buses that moved around the city were becoming more and

more covered in rust. The curtains on the windows no longer gave that same comfort and in general there were almost none left. There were no flowers in the flowerbeds because the watering system had not been installed. Poplars covered the whole city with fluff and it felt like summer had become winter. During the day the city died from impossible heat. The asphalt warmed up, the trees dried out, the churches remained unfinished, and near the two city hospitals people stood in queues from six in the morning. Sand lifted dust from the ground. Open windows in Zhiguli cars and music passed through me. My father’s shops with advertisements and discounts were also part of that city. When I was at school I would stop by one of his shops on the way home. There I would take a drink called Zhyvchyk, a sweet drink in a yellow metal can. When I came home my yard seemed smaller. The red brick house itself seemed smaller too. They were cutting down the forest to build new cottages. Most likely they dug up my secret treasure. In fourth grade I was fascinated by something black, bad, magical and dark. I always chose the side of evil. Once I went to Paris with my mother and my little brother. It was probably 2006. The walls of our room were covered with fabric and the room itself was very small. There was a staircase leading upstairs to a double bed where my brother and I slept. There was a small television inside the wardrobe and I watched Titanic in French. At night I woke up, looked out of the window, and there she was: a huge moon and the Eiffel Tower sparkling with lights. Since then I felt like a werewolf. When I came back home I told everyone that I could not be in the sun. Then I drew some kind of hieroglyphs very quickly in my notebook, found bones, stones and a small black box. I put all that little ritual material inside, went to the forest and buried it. Now my treasure is probably somewhere under the wheels of a bulldozer. The fruit on the trees was already getting ripe. I watered them every other day, bitten by mosquitoes, but I gave them a lot of water because I felt sorry leaving them under

122 123

the burning sun. That city seemed so understandable to me, so studied and small. The only thing that really motivated me to come back there was my grandmother L’s borscht. I rang her intercom without warning her that I was coming. Sometimes I spoke in a voice she did not recognize right away. The elevator to the fifth floor was still the same, with dim light and panels imitating wood texture. My grandmother was already standing by the door, waiting for me and hugging me tightly. She always had borscht ready, garlic, onion, cold salo, a crust of bread and tea. Black tea, brewed not in a mug but in a small bowl. That was how my father drank tea, and that way tea really tasted better. Sugar, no milk, strong brew. My father also loved making hot sandwiches. Sausage, ketchup, mayonnaise, garlic, and then all of it went into the oven. They baked, then cooled down, and a crust appeared on top. Those sandwiches were so popular that my friends at school knew about them. I sat with my grandmother for a long time. We talked, gossiped, and I looked at old photographs of relatives. Her old Soviet dishes, porcelain, books and Russian literature stood arranged by colour on the shelves of a huge cabinet. The flowers were lush, the clock was ticking, dried rose petals lay in a jar as if they were still waiting for us to take a bath again. But we had already grown up. Then I went to my other grandmother, who lived about twenty minutes away. Grandmother V. and grandfather V. She was always emotional and almost ready to cry when she saw me. My two grandmothers were definitely different in character and in how they saw life. The kettle was already boiling. Here tea was served in a mug, and instead of sugar there was always a bag of sweets. It was so easy to laugh with her. Her laughter was contagious. The pictures she embroidered and the beaded flowers kept growing in number, and she showed them to me every time. She often gave me her handmade things for my birthday, very carefully and with feeling, and she always noticed if her flowers disappeared from the shelves in our house. And on our shelves in the living room and dining room

there was always too much decor, dishes and souvenirs that created dust and visual noise. I liked everything minimal and laconic, so sometimes I carried some things into the storage room. Some members of my family did not like that. They sold the village house a long time ago. I remember that moment. I was little and sitting in the same yellow Zhiguli. The adults were moving around and I did not understand what was happening. It was evening and I was sitting in the car behind the gates of the house. Then we left. Nobody told me that the house had been sold. It happened because my grandparents no longer had the strength to look after the garden and the animals. I had grown up too, so most likely I would not have continued spending time in the village anyway. My summer adventures moved to Turkey, Egypt and Crimea. I also returned to Enerhodar because I wanted to see some of my girlfriends. It helped me distract myself from work and loneliness in Odesa. When you come home after visiting your grandmothers, after walking through evening Enerhodar, it no longer seems so scary. It feels as if it accepts you. You look at people a little differently, and inside you there is more confidence and more understanding of something in the world. My father had already lit the grill, the logs were slowly burning, he was adding coal, and the meat marinated since morning was already being put onto skewers. My father often went to the market in the morning on weekends. I remember once I climbed into the trunk of the car and he did not know about it. He drove to his office, and I was a little scared not to frighten him and not to frighten myself with his reaction. It became even scarier when he started speaking to one of his employees with swear words. No, he was not shouting at him. It was just his usual way of speaking. So, the grill. I loved looking at the fire. My eyes were already getting hot, but I still kept looking deep inside it, as if there was lava in there. My pupils became large, goosebumps went over my body, and above me there were bright stars. My father always cooked well, and my grandmother’s adjika only

124 125

made the grilled shashlik taste even better. Evening, the stadium, metal benches, grasshoppers chirping, many stars and a clear sky. In some windows of the buildings there was yellow and pink light. Groups of people often gathered at the stadium. Someone would take a guitar, play a chord, and you would sing along to the cult song “Batareyka” by Zhuki with the whole stadium. Goosebumps went over my body, and it felt like such a big future was still ahead.

I studied who fought with whom, who betrayed whom, who signed which treaty and where each battle took place. I and N. from Enerhodar ended up in Enerhodar again. To be honest, that period during quarantine felt somehow strangely relaxed and accepted to me. We went to the sauna almost every day. What were you thinking, father? My mother confirmed that it was her. I was already in the room then, and so much anger was boiling inside me that I went back to the beach. I walked quickly, holding my sneakers in my hand, squeezing them into a fist. I went up to her. “R, is that you?” She turned around, and I hit her in the face with the sneaker. If not for my politeness, intelligence and upbringing, I would not have stopped and would have hit her again. What a shame that it was only once. She said my name with that horrible mouth of hers, softly, almost affectionately: “Please, Stasik, we need to talk, let’s talk.” I left and went to my father’s room. of him. You are pathetic to me, father. You will not be the one shouting at me anymore. Now you will learn that I can do it too. He opened the door. I said, “What the hell is she doing here?
