New Year was almost here, and I was decorating the Christmas tree in Enerhodar. You know how it feels every time: these traditions of decorating rooms, taking the tree out of the storage room, spreading it out after it has been lying in a box for a whole year, making it fuller. The same ornaments serve as decorations year after year, sometimes new angels or glowing garlands appear. I always caught myself thinking how sad it was that there seemed to be no common tradition like that anymore. Everyone

is busy with their own things, worries, problems, and there is no longer that feeling that the world becomes one whole thing for a moment. Everything is moving more and more into digital, and maybe only the Coca-Cola Christmas ads remind you that New Year is coming. Maybe I am being too dramatic. My father decorated our garden with bright garlands. If you looked from the second floor, the whole yard glowed with colorful lights. Our table was already covered with candles, and my mother was taking her signature roasted chicken out of the oven. My mother always did matte makeup, emphasized her brown eyes with black pencil, and her gaze became even brighter. Curled hair, red lipstick. The chimes struck, and I wrote all my wishes on a piece of paper and set it on fire. The main thing was to make it in time. Drink the champagne in one gulp, while the paper was barely swallowed in your mouth. My father hinted to my mother that she should go look for her present under the tree. It was a Rolex watch covered in diamonds. Of course I tried it on myself. I often tried on my mother’s diamonds. There is something attractive in those stones. But did it make my mother happy? Was she happy with my father? The doorbell rang, and the first guests came to congratulate us. They often gave my brother and me money in envelopes. That smell of a fur coat after frost — there is probably no better scent. Was my father congratulating that mistress at that moment too, while we were all together at the table? We went outside to watch my father light the fireworks. Grandmother L often said: “Money into the air.” She was difficult to understand. She was a complicated person and often said things that my aunt or my mother did not like. I think she often felt lonely, even though she had three sons. She always complained about my father, although he supported her financially in every possible way. Maybe she needed something else from him. Not money, but warmth. She was quite vulnerable, but very close to me. Those intimate late-night gatherings that gave me goosebumps, with a candle on the table, when you talk about something real and drink tea with a piece

168 169

of hard cheese. Her warm hands giving me a massage, and her gentle voice saying: “My grandson.” She had aged so much and started complaining about problems with her legs, although it seemed like only recently she had been taking me to playgrounds, and we had traveled together to visit her relatives in Rostov. We slept in hotels, rode trains, lay on the beach. That train sound: tuhtuh. I am lying on the shelf in the train compartment and listening: tuh-tuh. It felt like only recently she was picking me up from school and making pancakes. You know, it is hard for me to write about this now, because I am moving myself into the past, while at this very moment my grandmother has become even older. I cannot open all the curtains yet, because this is not that moment. We have not reached it yet. But it is very hard for me to write about her now. New Year. Here comes my other grandmother V. with her husband V. She often brought candies in gift boxes shaped like little houses or animals. The same boxes that Ded Moroz used to bring us at our performances in primary school. The same gifts that my father sorted at his warehouse. I even took part in it once. The love I felt during my first encounters, full of shame and fear of being exposed, and the love I came to know beside a person who saw me entirely, are not two levels of the same feeling. They are different abilities, requiring different amounts of honesty with yourself. Love transforms because the person who feels it transforms. In the beginning, love almost always looks like salvation. You find someone, and it seems as if they take away all the weight you had been carrying alone. This is the most tempting stage, and the most deceptive one, because the person you love cannot take away your weight. Later, love becomes a mirror. This is the most unpleasant stage, because the mirror shows not only your partner, but also you, with all your jealousy, anxiety, and fear of being abandoned. It is exactly at this stage that people most often decide that love was a mistake, although it has simply finally shown the truth that is easier not to see when you are alone. And if you go further, and few people do, because it requires staying in the relationship with your eyes open instead of running away the moment the mirror becomes uncomfortable, love becomes a choice. Does love necessarily have to hurt? Pain in love is almost never the pain of love itself. It is the pain of an old fear that love has finally illuminated. Analyze your parents, and it will turn out that you often repeat the scripts of your mother or father. Love, if you strip it of all inherited fear, is not about the disappearance of pain, and not about its inevitability either. It is about the ability to stand beside another person without needing either to dissolve into them or protect yourself from them. Goodness almost always seems like something obvious and simple. We are taught this from childhood. We are taught to be kind, to help, not to hurt, not to get angry, not to destroy. But the older we become, the more clearly we understand that goodness rarely looks as pure and clear as it does in children’s stories. Goodness can speak in a soft voice, and sometimes it comes in the form of strength. Is the winner the one who is good, or is goodness only a mask of victory? The winner almost always becomes the one who decides where good was and where evil was. But inside every person, there remains a feeling that truth is not so simple. You can win a war and lose your humanity. You can lose and keep your dignity. Sometimes victory is only a beautiful word hiding exhaustion, destroyed families, lives, and emptiness. That is why victory itself can never be proof of goodness. A person often puts on the mask of virtue. Not because he is necessarily lying, but because it is comfortable to be good. People love those who look right. People trust those who say the right words. It creates safety, respect, and recognition. But under this mask, there is often fear, the desire to be accepted, the desire not to be left alone. And then goodness becomes not an inner choice, but a social role. We are afraid of tall grass because there may be poisonous snakes hiding there. But reality is more complicated. Sometimes it is the opposite. Those who constantly speak about love can

340 341

be more poisonous than those who look dangerous. Those people may have more humanity than those who constantly display their softness. Even a person who has done monstrous things remains human. This does not make him innocent, but it shows the complexity of human nature. Evil is created by people, not monsters. A person who commits evil does not stop being human. He remains a person who made a choice, who destroyed the boundaries inside himself and allowed cruelty to become normal. This does not justify him. On the contrary, it makes his responsibility even heavier. Because evil is not committed by some abstract monster, but by a person who could have chosen differently. A person and humanity are not the same thing. A person can exist biologically and socially, while almost completely destroying within himself the ability to feel compassion, responsibility, and empathy. He remains human by nature, but his actions can become deeply anti-human. So the question is not so much whether a person crosses the boundaries of the human. It is more that he destroys inside himself what makes a person human. And then a tragic paradox appears. Evil does not come from outside. It is born inside human nature when a person stops limiting his own power over others. Pain makes a person calm, cold. But coldness does not mean he has no heart. Anger also rarely appears out of nothing. A person does not become cruel for no reason. Anger is often born from exhaustion, from helplessness, from an inner struggle that no one sees. Hatred seems to be directed outward, at us, but in reality, it destroys the one who carries it. A person full of hatred lives next to his own fire. The strictest judgment happens inside us. Love leaves. Anger and hatred dissolve. Words that once seemed important lose their power. If everything passes, what remains? People remain. They ask the same questions again. They look again for the boundary between strength and humanity. They try again to understand how to live beside one another without destroying the world around them. Every generation begins this conversation again. A person can justify himself before others, can find

thousands of explanations for his actions, but inside there is always a quiet voice that knows the truth. It is that small child inside us.
